The word "sedition" is not and cannot be defined and is not defined in any of our statutes. It is an indefinable offence; as has been stated time and again in this house,

sedition depends very largely upon the time and place the act is committed or the statement is made. When we look back over some of the things that the crown have claimed to be seditious within the last few years I think it must be agreed that a most ridiculous interpretation has been placed on section 98 of the criminal code. I should like to indicate what some people in Canada have said on which they have been charged with sedition:
Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed;
To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widow's may be their prey and that they may rob the fatherless.
The following words also were part of the charge against a person whose name I will mention in a moment:
And they shall build houses and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them.	_
They shall not build, and another inhabit; they shall not plant, and another eat: for as the days of a tree are the days of my people, and mine elect shall long enjoy the work of their hands.
Those are quotations from the book of Isaiah, yet it was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who was 'accused of sedition in the courts of this country for quoting from the bible what I have just read. That was done under section 98 of the criminal code, and if it was done ait that- time it is quite possible it might be done again if the section remains.
Some of my hon. friends are timid about individuals using language which might be regarded as seditious. After all, who ultimately is the judge of what is seditious? Is it not for a jury to decide? Who is the final jury? Is it not the people of Canada? In 1919 a number of people in Winnipeg were charged with seditious utterances and seditious conspiracy and were convicted of that charge, yet immediately after their conviction they were returned by enormous majorities to the legislature of Manitoba. They were elected to that legislature while they were incarcerated in the gaols of that province. And the present mayor of Winnipeg, who has been elected for two terms by fairly large majorities, majorities representative of all the people of that city, is one who was sentenced to gaol for seditious conspiracy in 1920. The thing becomes ridiculous when a few people set themselves up as judges of the law and send people to gaol who after all represent the viewpoint and convictions of a majority of the people of any community.

Criminal Code-Mr. Wilton
It has been claimed by some that we should not allow certain statements to be made. There are, I think, no hon. members of this house who believe in the advocacy of physical force. I think we are all opposed to that. The very fact that we run candidates in elections, that we try through our limited means to bring the majority of people in Canada to our way of thinking, is in itself a vindication of our ideas on this question. But we do say that if you want to stop people from giving vent to seditious utterances the best way to do it is to remove the causes of dissatisfaction. At the present time there are a good many causes for people in this country to be dissatisfied, yet we find very little advocacy of force from any source, even from the communist party.
Ideas cannot be killed by force. If an idea is not worthwhile it will die, and ideas that are worthwhile will grow in spite of all opposition; for in the final analysis that which is right and logical is bound to come out on top. Ideas are like a seed planted in the ground. If the seed is good and it has the sunshine it will sprout and grow, perhaps into a beautiful flower; but if the seed is bad the same sunshine will kill it. Let all ideas come out into the open and I am satisfied that ultimately the logic and good sense of the people will determine what is right and what is wrong. If we try with any sedition laws to suppress freedom of speech it is a grievous mistake; consequently I am glad that the Minister of Justice and the government have taken the responsibility of doing away with section 98. But I regret to observe that while doing away with section 98, in which there are certain definitions as to what the authorities may do, they bring in a wide clause the interpretation of which is so indefinite and uncertain that I would ask the Minister of Justice at a later stage to state to the house whether he himself can give an interpretation of what the clause actually means.
The second line of the new clause reads:
... every one shall be presumed to have a seditious intention ...
Does that mean that a person who may be charged under this clause is presumed to be guilty?
No.

Well, that depends entirely on the interpretation that is placed upon it by the judge. According to my understanding of the interpretation given to it even by lawyers, it is that the presumption of guilt is upon the accused instead of its being incumbent upon the prosecution to prove him guilty.
12739-249 J
It is also unfortunate that "force" has not been more clearly defined. Again if is a question of interpretation. In 1920 a glance would have been interpreted by a judge in Manitoba as the use of force. I am wondering whether the law as we have it without this subsection 4 would not have been sufficient to cover the situation. There are quite a number of sections in the existing law that would take care of a person who advocates the use of force for the overthrow of government. It is a mistake to put into any act a clause such as this, so ambiguous and capable of being interpreted in so many different ways. Perhaps when we come to the committee stage the Minister of Justice will be good enough to give to the committee his interpretation of this particular section, because for myself, having at times listened to the interpretation of sedition by judges and lawyers, I have a feeling that if a person were brought before the courts of this country and charged under subsection 4 he would be likely to have as much difficulty in proving his innocence as he might have had under section 98.

Following the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth), for whom I have a very high personal regard, I should like to make a few comments on what he said. The hon. member says he does not agree with all the policies of the communists-one noted his emphasis on the word "all." Personally I find it very hard to understand how any good Canadian citizen can agree with anything that the communist party stands for in Canada or elsewhere, a party whose chief aim and object is the overthrow of organized government and absolute disrespect for law and order.
It seems to me the only people who need to fear section 98 are those who are likely to break it. Reference was made by the hon. member who preceded me to a mayor who had been sentenced to gaol because of a breach of this section. I do not know why even a mayor should be exempt from the laws; if he breaks them he should be penalized. We do not make our laws only for the common man, or the man in a lower position, and there is no reason why we should exempt the mayor of any city.
He was not mayor at the time he was sentenced.
You said so.
No.

My knowledge of communistic effort has been extensive because I have come into close contact with it in public-
Criminal Code-Mr. Wilton

municipal life. Having watched its development over a period of two or three years I know something about the organization. I know they hold secret meetings in private homes; I know they are teaching their children to have no respect for law and order. They are advocating everything that is disrespectful to the social structure and laws of our country. When the police are not watching they distribute seditious literature, which is prepared for them in a basement headquarters within a stone's throw of Times square, New York. That literature is transmitted to them by some means throughout different parts of Canada where their efforts are concentrated. It is found on city streets in the mornings. They come out of their places like rats out of holes in the middle of the night, and distribute it throughout the cities. They post boys at factory gates to hand it to the workers, and they get away with it until they are caught by the police. Those are the people whom section 98 is designed to cover. No law abiding, self-respecting Canadian citizen need fear section 98. The communist party as I know it and as I have seen it operate are leeches on society in every manner, shape and form of which it is possible to conceive. They refuse to acknowledge allegiance to their king; they stand in groups in public places and refuse to remove their hats when the national anthem is sung; they bury their dead without religious rites, and they ignore everything that is decent and right in the laws of our land.
There is a tendency on the part of many good citizens to treat the communist agitation lightly. Some say, "Oh, why raise an agitation? They are not very strong; they cannot do much harm; perhaps it is better to leave them alone. Let them say what they like and do as they like; they will never be able to become the law makers of Canada or break the structure of our legal system. Why bother with them"? I feel keenly in this matter, and I urge that it is one to be considered seriously. It is a matter of much more serious import than the average Canadian realizes. Many years ago a man named Noah walked about on the face of the earth telling the people to come into his ark, that it was going to rain. He told them there was going to be a flood and that they would be drowned. They laughed at him and called him an old fool. When he began building the ark they gathered around and watched him, persisting in calling him an old fool. But when they were in water up to their necks, standing on the highest points they could reach, they realized the truth of Noah's statement.

Not many years ago a man named Lloyd George stood in his place in the British parliament and warned parliament against the war preparations of Germany which were being carried on under the very nose of that parliament. They laughed at Lloyd George; but when they were in mire and muck up to their knees, and when they stood in the blood of their fellow human beings, they realized that little Lloyd George had been telling them the truth.
The red movement in Canada is a menace which must be taken seriously, if we are to prevent the downfall of responsible government. No loyal Canadian wants to see the downfall of Canadian government; we prefer law, order and civilization. But we are heading for a downfall unless we treat the red menace seriously and do not choose to sit back and laugh at it. The red menace in Canada is not to be laughed at. People now living will live to see and realize its seriousness. There are those who say that red policies will never come in our time. I say they are coming in ouy time unless we are prepared to take the menace seriously.
Section 98 of the criminal code is in existence to take care of those who defy our law, who defy our social progress and who would tear down and wreck our civilization. I say to hon. members that the red movement is a menace within reach of us; it is something against which we must protect the public and our children, otherwise we may go through the same process as did the people in Noah's day.

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Wilton) referred to Noah's invitation to the people of his day to come into the ark lest they be faced with chaos brought about by a flood, I could not help recalling what took place during the last election campaign. It was said that those who did not vote for the Liberal party would be faced with chaos.

They took the
warning this time, but they did not in Noah's time.

Let us
interpret the word "chaos." It seems to me that chaos would indicate a chaotic state, and a chaotic state must necessarily be one in which there is terrorism. As I read the section I wonder why some who preached the doctrine to which I have referred were not prosecuted under it. Well, that did not happen. My point is that because of the ambiguity of the section and its multiplicity of words and expressions, it could be made

Criminal Code-Mr. Johnston
applicable to almost any one or any condition, and I believe the government should be commended most highly upon repealing it. In my opinion it is a violation of private privileges. It seems to me to be in the nature of a warlike emergency, as was intimated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I do not think we are so much in danger of anything so terrible as some speakers would have us believe as to need the drastic warlike emergency measure contained in section 98. There is another thing that should be considered. The power is given to the police to appoint anyone to go into a private residence to confiscate literature. The home is the sacred possession of every citizen, and as this section now stands, homes may be invaded by outsiders on practically any excuse they may wish to present. This certainly needs repealing.
Paragraph 4 of section 98 refers to meetings. I am of the opinion that it would be hard to enter any meeting which in some way did not come under this section. This practically prohibits anyone advocating a change in the form of government. During the last election there was considerable cry for reform, especially monetary reform. Some very strong statements were made by all parties in connection with this. There were some very strong references by the Liberal party to the Conservative administration, and ' similar statements were made by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in regard to both the Liberals and the Conservatives. Social crediters had something to say about all the others, and I think it was coming to them. It is hard to tell just how serious all these statements might have been when considered in the light of section 98.
As I listened to the speeches this afternoon I was convinced that the purpose of this section was to get after the so-called communists. I should like to make it quite clear that this party is not associated in any manner or form with socialism of communism. That being so, we have nothing to fear from section 98, but our endeavour is to see that all citizens are treated fairly. One of the most essential things in a democratic country is freedom of speech. If we represent a policy which is so weak that it cannot stand the test of argument and fair debate, then I think it will automatically go down. It is the consensus of opinion that all these subjects should be debated from all angles. If this section is allowed to remain, I believe it will curtail the expression of opinion and thought. As the minister indicated not so long ago, a man should not be condemned for expressing an opinion, but he should be punished for deeds and acts. I
do not think this is made clear in the legis lation under review.
I did not intend to deal with this matter at any great length, because it has been gone over pretty thoroughly. But I think I should say something in view of the fact that I have received so many representations from different groups and organizations all over Alberta and in other parts of Canada. I have had complaints from labour organizations. I have attended the meetings of a great many labour organizations, and with the exception of one, held in Banff about a year ago, I never heard any indication whatever of violence. Reforms of one kind and another were advocated, but only on the one occasion did I hear anything that could be interpreted to be at all in the form of violence. I think this legislation could have been applied to that particular meeting I have had representations from railway employees' organizations in different parts of Alberta, and I do not believe anyone can accuse those men of any criminal intent or anything of that kind. I have had them from farmers' organizations, and I have had them from individuals in every occupation.
After I read section 4 of the bill I went down to the library where I found a great many socialistic books. I read1 portions of them, some of which were similar to those referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The thought came to my mind that if this section were allowed to stand the library and all those associated with it would necessarily come under its provisions. The section refers to those who circulate such literature. Many of the news stands and those people who publish periodicals of different kinds would come under this section if a literal interpretation were put upon it.
Perhaps it might not be well to have this bill sent back to the committee to be reconsidered, but the minister should give some consideration to this section. I think the original intention of section 98 was to apply to any extreme acts, and perhaps insufficient consideration was given to the wording. With a little further thought it seems to me it could be changed to cover fully such actions as have been mentioned.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the character of the debate I feel I should make at least a few remarks. May I say at once that the maintenance of national liberty is dependent upon the restraint of individual liberty. That is a strange statement which at first may appear to be contradictory, but it is not. There oan be no such thing as the maintenance of national liberty among the peoples of this country unless there is a
Criminal Code-Mr. Bennett

restraint of individual liberty. Further, the extent to which the nation enjoys freedom and liberty depends upon the extent to which restraint is carried out. If the restraint is undue upon individual liberty, then there is resentment. On the other hand, if it is inadequate, liberty becomes licence. I do not think it can be gainsaid that that is a fair statement of the situation.
Further, the laws which thus restrain the individual liberty for the well being of the nation as a whole are enacted not for the law abiding citizen but as restraints upon citizens who would convert liberty into licence. We have a statute which was passed in 1919, some seventeen years ago, which is still in full force and efficiency. During the last few years it has been openly defied because under our jurisdiction the provinces must maintain criminal proceedings. The dominion can only take certain preliminary steps, and it rests with the attorneys general of the provinces to say whether or not the law shall be carried into effect.
In the midst of political disturbance and difference it frequently happens that men ally themselves to a particular course of action from which they find it exceedingly difficult to separate themselves when their better reason and stronger judgment tell them they should. I have read declarations with respect to section 98 on the part of those charged with responsibility, stating what course they would pursue, and I know perfectly well that in their saner and calmer moments those who made the declaration, if they were correctly reported, would have had no intention to aid and succour and abet those who had been openly defying the law. During the last few years we have had open expressions of defiance of the law. In the leading case to which reference was made this morning by the minister, namely, the Buck case, Chief Justice Mulock, speaking for the whole appellate division of the Ontario court, indicated that the opinion of that court was that what had transpired constituted an offence under the provisions of section 98. Let us see whether or not we have any adequate safeguards outside of that statute-I am talking about the substantive provisions of it. What does it indicate? May I answer that question by saying that it does not indicate anything that the people have been led to believe it does. There has been so much misrepresentation as to what this section means-because in the very nature of things it is somewhat longer than a statute intended to convey that meaning ordinarily would be-that I am sure there

has been a great deal of misapprehension on the part of many people. First of all it aims at unlawful associations; and the Chief Justice of Ontario pointed out that we had in Canada determined, by the verdict of a jury as well as by the admissions made by those who were charged and who in some instances conducted their own defence, that it took its direction from another organization, which organization had its foundations and its home in a foreign land, and that it was part of the declared purpose of that organization to effectuate by force the ends intended or purposed. Notwithstanding what my opponents may say to the contrary, none of us for a single moment desire to restrict or curb liberty of speech. The address of Erskine, the advocate, is hardly conclusive as to the judicial interpretation of a statute. Erskine, the advocate, was one of the greatest of his time, but in arguing his case upon the evidence submitted to a jury it can hardly be contended that he is making declarations of high principles of law. In the advocacy of the so-called iniquities of section 98 men have been led to believe that it is much more harmful and restrictive than is necessary to maintain national liberty. Let us look at it for a moment:
Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advises or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, in order to accomplish such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed purpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful association.
I venture to think that in the quiet calm of his own home, if I were discussing the matter with any hon. member sitting opposite me who thinks differently than I do on large public questions, he wouid say, "I think it is a perfectly sound and proper thing, Mr. Bennett, that we should have this definition of unlawful assemblies or associations; and I agree with you, Mr. Bennett, that there should be a law against men carrying on, by association, efforts to destroy by force and violence and injury to persons the institutions of the country." I feel perfectly certain that my bitterest opponent opposite, in the quiet calm of a room discussing the matter, would agree that this is desirable-highly desirable.
The next section deals with a matter of procedure with which I am not in sympathy

Criminal Code-Mr. Bennett
and never have been since the end of the war, because it provides for the seizing and forfeiture of property on the warrant of the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That is not the general purpose of our law, to clothe an official with that authority under a special aft of this significance. But what amused me was this. One would think that there were no such similar provisions in the laws of the country. What about gaming devices? What about houses of ill repute? What about the question of the right of police officers and chiefs of police to seize property, with or without a search warrant in some cases? What about the issue of warrants by magistrates, justices of the peace, and judges of county courts? All these things are provided for in the statute. To us some of them seem trifling because our attention has never been directed to them, but they have been there ever since we have endeavoured by statute to clarify the criminal common law since the days we started, in 1892, to codify the law consequent upon the report primarily of a British commission and the work of Sir James Fitzstephen. But leaving that out, I wonder whether hon. members would take the trouble to turn up the code and look at the sections with respect to search warrants, the right to enter a property and seize things, to arrest people, and matters of that kind. All this is so simple that we take it for granted and do not for a moment give thought to it when we are dealing with section 98.
Subsection 2 of section 98, to which I have just referred, is am extraordinary section, and my personal view would be that as a matter of procedure, in view of present conditions, it would be better if it were removed. But when we come to subsection 3, which relates to persons who act as officers of these unlawful associations, does anyone suggest that it is not. desirable to have punitive power, so far as this country is concerned!, with respect to them?-not so much for the purpose of punishing in the first instance as for the purpose of ensuring, by placing on the statute books this legislation restricting our individual liberty to that extent, that the nation as a whole may have that measure of liberty which is synonymous with our institutions. Then you go to the next: what constitutes evidence of membership in an association. That is a matter that is debatable. Whether or not these clauses are adequate, or whether we might not amplify them, as to what constitutes evidence that one is a member of an association, I will not further labour. But these provisions of that subsection indicate that if certain conditions exist there is a presumption that a man is
a member of that association, a presumption that may ibe rebutted by cogent evidence.
Subsection 5 is only an amplification of what we have had as the law of the country for a very long time. If a man rents a house knowing that it is to be used for prostitution, he cannot recover rent. That is fairly clear amd the reason is obvious. If he rents his house for the purpose of having it used as a gambling joint, he is in the same position, and we have merely said in this subsection that the owner of a build'-ing who knowingly .permits meetings to be held in it for the promotion-the promotion, mark you-of the destruction of our institutions, by force and injury to people, makes himself liable. But he must have knowledge, and unless you can prove that he has knowledge there is no responsibility. In other words, it is the old story:	If a man
has knowledge of the fact that certain things are to be done, improperly or illegally, or that certain property of his is to be used for improper or illegal purposes, he cannot escape the result of his own acts, and we have here said that he should be liable.
Subsection 6, which also is a matter of procedure, provides for a search warrant being issued, and there is nothing in that subsection that derogates from the general principles with respect to the issue of search warrants. It is a statement of the conditions under which a search warrant may be issued for a given purpose.
There follow further provisions in clause 7 as to the procedure to be adopted. Then you pass into the realm of sedition, about which the minister was speaking this morning. Here we have provisions against the publication of seditious books and the circulation of books and newspapers, and obviously, if we are going to have these provisions, against the importation of such books and newspapers. The next clause deals with the duty of government employees, who have had brought to their attention evidences of the commission of the offences to which I have referred, to take immediate steps to remedy the conditions so far as it may be within their power so to do.
Apart only from the procedure indicated in the subclause to which I specially directed attention, is there anything in section 98 which reasonable citizens should desire to have removed? Is there in this chamber any reasonable citizen who will say: I am not prepared to make that sacrifice of my individual liberty for the preservation of the liberty of the state as a whole? That is the test. Is there a single individual sitting
Criminal Code-Mr. Bennett

here who will say: It is not right that I should make this surrender of my unquestionable complete liberty for the purpose of advancing the interests of the nation and which I do in the manner that is indicated, by passing this statute? It is true that some of our friends connected with labour organizations at one time believed this section capable of being used against strikes, and I understand that a legal opinion was given that there was some question of that kind. I have always said, and I repeat, that if there were any doubt upon that point it could easily be removed, but for my own part I believe, and I think the law officers of the crown, that is the Department of Justice, were clear on the matter, that there is nothing therein contained that could be regarded, by any possible stretching of language, as capable of being utilized against those engaged in a strike which under our law is lawful.
The minister proposes to repeat the section in its entirety. If his purpose were to amend it along the lines I have suggested, or any lines that his judgment might indicate as being more desirable, I would not for a moment question it. But in these days is it desirable to repeal that section? Take this city of Ottawa. On the staff of Ottawa university is a very learned professor who has given a great deal of time to the investigation of this situation, and whose pamphlets are worth reading. I wonder if it is known to what extent there exists in this very city, according to evidence that is now available, if any hon. member desires to ascertain by investigation what the situation is, a condition to meet which certain associations are being promoted and men are giving of their money to combat to the best of their ability. In one or two parts of this city will be found what are known as friendship houses, which are endeavouring to improve the situation by bringing home an adequate appreciation of conditions to the minds of those who are filled with, shall I say, very extreme views as to the desirability of remedying by force present day conditions.
There would have been no progress in this world unless there had been freedom of speech, unless the ideas of men of broad vision had been communicated to their fellows. The communication of ideas which are advanced, extreme, radical, has never been restrained in this country unless the direct result has been that which is contemplated by sections 131 and 136 inclusive of our law, that is sedition. This morning the minister was speaking on the subject of sedition. As a matter of fact we have on our statute book

to-day a law against seditious words, which are punishable by imprisonment up to two years. The minister complained that under section 98 the punishment is extreme. But the punishment is only what may be, not what has to be, and when you say that a man "may" be punished by imprisonment for twenty years you might just as well have said forty, as far as the section is concerned, because the discretion rests with the court, after a verdict of guilty has been found, as to what the measure of the punishment shall be. In the case of those to whom he alluded this morning the punishment, of course, was far removed from twenty years.
I am correcting only one thing the minister said during his remarks to-day. He said that Buck was released by the same government or kind of government that was responsible for this section. I believe on analysis he will find that that is not quite correct. What happened in Buck's case is an exemplification of the very principle to which I have referred, that one prisoner should not be treated differently from another because of the character of the offence for which he has been committed. Buck was committed under section 98. He was in the penitentiary. The report on his case was just the same as on a man who was convicted, let us say, for stealing. The report was of good conduct within the terms of the penitentiary regulations, and when a prisoner has served half his term, which is the usual time, whether the conviction be for theft or for any other offence, if the other conditions have been complied with, the executive power has the privilege, which under regulation is the general rule, of giving him a ticket of leave or permitting him to be released on parole. That was done with Buck. It was done for two reasons: one, because he came within the regulations; two, because if he had been treated differently from others it would at once have afforded an opportunity for those- who desired to say, and who prepared themselves to say, by communications they sent to the government of the day, that we were treating this man differently from other prisoners and that we, the executive, were imposing upon him a punishment that was not imposed upon other prisoners lodged in the penitentiary who had earned for themselves a ticket of leave or release on parole. Unfortunately I happen to know that that is the attitude that was taken by those who had to deal with him in that respect.
Under these circumstances we ask ourselves whether a case has been made out for the repeal of the section, or for its revision. Along

Criminal Code-Mr. Bennett
the lines indicated by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), embodying views which I think have been held by many of us for a long time, it may well be that the procedure could be improved, and that with regard to the power conferred upon the commissioner of the mounted police it could be said with great truth that in these days, a long time after the condition that existed in 1918 or 1919, a search warrant issued in the ordinary way would be ample protection of the people of the country as a whole.
There remains one other matter. In 1928 the same minister who is now Minister of Justice was dealing with this matter. I think he said that he had moved five or six times that the section should be repealed. At that time he proposed to restore the section which dealt with freedom of speech. He said, on April 23, 1928, page 2303 of Hansard:
At the same time section 133 which existed at that time was repealed and I intend to move an amendment in order to reinsert section 133. This was done last year and in the years previously, and it is only due to a mistake that this bill did not contain that provision. I think the house will see that parliament obviously went too far in 1919 when the section which I am now going to read was repealed.
That section reads as follows:
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith,-
(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the United Kingdom ... ; or
(c)	to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing or have a tendency to produce feelings of hatred and ill-will between different classes of His Majesty's subjects.
If we look at the law as it now stands, Mr. Speaker, we find that since then there has been a change to some extent and that the sections dealing with seditious offences are sections 130 and following. Section 133a is now part of the criminal code of Canada, and in terms it is substantially the same as the amendments the Minister of Justice proposed to move in 1928. Section 133a reads:
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith,-
(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or,
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the United Kingdom, or of any part of it, or of Canada or any province thereof, or in either house of parliament of the United Kingdom or of Canada, or in any legislature, or in the administration of justice; or to excite His Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in the state; or,
(c)	to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing or have a tendency to produce feelings of hatred and ill-will between different classes of His Majesty's subjects.
That is a part of the criminal law of Canada, and therefore it is unnecessary to reenact it. That was placed in our statutes in 1930. But the minister, no doubt intending to say, "I have repealed section 98 but I have enacted a provision that will be equally effective," proposes to provide for cases of sedition under the sections to which I have referred. I do not agree with the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) that under any circumstances this section can be regarded as equivalent to section 98, for section 98 does a great and useful purpose by defining unlawful associations and providing methods of dealing with them. Section 130 and the following sections deal only with seditious offences; that is the heading in the criminal code. After defining the various offences for which adequate punishment is provided we find the following words in section 133:
Seditious words are words expressive of a seditious intention.
2.	A seditious libel is a libel expressive of a seditious intention.
3.	A seditious conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to carry into execution a seditious intention.
Now the minister proposes to add, as paragraph 4, these words:
(4) Without limiting the generality of the meaning of the expression "seditious intention" everyone shall be presumed to have a seditious intention who publishes, or circulates any writing, printing or document in which it is advocated, or who teaches or advocates, the use, without the authority of law, of force, as a means of accomplishing any governmental change.
In other words by this proposed subsection we create a presumption that anyone who does what is indicated here is guilty of a seditious intention. That is, anyone who (1) publishes; (2) circulates (a) writing (b) printing or (c) a document in which it is advocated, or who teaches ot advocates the use, without the authority of law, of force as a means of accomplishing any governmental change, shall be presumed to have a seditious intention. That, of course, is a rebuttable presumption but it places upon the man at once the onus of satisfying the court and jury, if there be a jury, that the intention which is presumed against him does not in fact exist. But that does not deal with the sections that have to do with unlawful associations. As was stated this morning, though not at length, by the former Secretary of State (Mr. Caban), these are illustrations but they do not constitute an all-embracing definition of sedition or of
Criminal Code-Mr. Bennett

seditious offences. The common law of England is elastic and not rigid in that sense, and when the effort was made in Great Britain, as in Canada, to provide a definition for sedition or seditious offences it was felt that to endeavour to confine these offences within the narrowing boundaries of a definition would be against the best interests of the state. Therefore we have left the common law provisions as they are, but in at least several instances we have undertaken to indicate what are within that definition. We have not defined but we have said that certain offences fall within that definition, and those offences are indicated by the law.
In section 98 as it now stands we have provisions with respect to unlawful associations and the activities of officers of such associations which I do submit in all sincerity should not be repealed at this time, though one might desire to repeal some of the provisions that deal with procedure in that regard.
That is all, Mr. Speaker, that I desire to say with respect to the matter. I protest against this change in these days of uncertainty and unrest, knowing as I do the conditions right in this city and knowing of the activities that are going on and how much those activities have been modified, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) said this afternoon. Why have those activities been modified? Because of the arrangement recently made between Russia and France. Apparently, according to the information that has been given me, instructions have been issued that there must be a modification of the attitude of the Third International and those who spoke for certain interests in Russia, as indicated in the judgment of Chief Justice Mulock in the Buck ease. That has been modified, and the reason is clearly apparent to everyone. But what assurance have we that that modification will continue? We have no assurance whatever, and the repeal of this legislation will be accepted by those who have been carrying on propaganda in this country so actively during the last four years as giving them added opportunities and greater scope for their seditious operations.
The finding, for instance, of the four judges in Saskatchewan should not be overlooked in this regard. That was a commission, certainly not friendly to the late administration by any stretch of the imagination; the conduct of the proceedings did not indicate any friendliness on the part of those responsible for it. But the finding of that commission-and I was surprised that they went as far as they did-made it perfectly clear that there existed a common purpose and that if

necessary force was to be relied upon to accomplish certain ends. In the light of that fact; in the light of the conditions that exist in this city to-day, to my knowledge and the knowledge of many members of this house; in the light of what we read from day to day of the literature that is circulating and the secret gatherings and meetings that are held, is it desirable to leave this country without any provision to take the place of section 98, if you do not like it in its entirety, with nothing that will have a similar effect in dealing with unlawful associations and those who are associated in the creation and maintenance of such association?
Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.
Does he believe that the penalties imposed by section 98 would be effective either to prevent or to arrest the growth of unlawful associations as defined by section 98?

I have not the slightest doubt that they have been and will continue to be, if they are allowed to continue on the statute book. I will agree at once if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) desires me to say that if I were drafting the statute I would not have set the penalty at a maximum of twenty years, but we know that penalties and sentences are wholly within the discretion of the judge who administers the sentence. I know also that in the case to which reference was made this morning the sentence was for a very much shorter period than the limit set by the statute. It does not follow, unless the statute says "not less than," that the sentence indicated has to be imposed. For instance, under the Post Office Act there is a very drastic provision which in some instances leaves no discretion to the court as to the sentence that must be given. But in this case it was left entirely free and in the discretion of the presiding judge to determine the punishment, the maximum being twenty years. As I said, it might just as well have been forty; for no judge would think it desirable to impose a sentence of twenty years for the offence in question. There is a disparity between the sentences under section 98 and those under the other sections of the act, but that cannot be taken to militate against its effectiveness.
When the minister asks whether I think the continuance of the section would have a salutary effect, I say yes, beyond peradven-ture. It is a matter of individual opinion. I may have drawn wrong conclusions from

Criminal Code-Mr. Bennett
the manifestations of what I regard as seditious activities which have come to my notice. I may draw a stronger conclusion than my hon. friend the Minister of Labour would draw. That is a matter of individual opinion. But there is one thing that is not a question of opinion: are these efforts being made? Does there exist in this country any assembly or body of men and women who are urging upon their fellow citizens that force should be used for the purpose of accomplishing their end? The answer obviously must be in the affirmative. I will undertake to prove to the Minister of Justice this very night in this city, if he will give me time and come with me, that they exist. It may be that their force and effect has been overstated; about that there may be difference of opinion. There is a tendency on the part of some to exaggerate their importance. I am not doing one or the other; I am not minimizing, nor am I magnifying. I state the fact. Now, under these conditions, should we leave the Dominion of Canada in 1936 without any provision against that type of unlawful assembly and those who constitute its membership? That is the real issue. The proposed subsection 4 of 133 does not touch that. It merely says that one who does certain things is presumed to have a seditious intention. But that does not touch this question at all.
I regret that the minister has seen fit to make so sweeping a change. Had he at an earlier point in the session afforded an opportunity for a more complete discussion I have little doubt that hon. members of this house on every side would have been glad to cooperate with him to the full in endeavouring to provide in an intelligent way against what I think every hon. member will admit is an evil. And getting back to my original observation, if it is thought that the provisions are too drastic, if the restraints imposed upon the individual are greater than are necessary for the purpose of maintaining liberty in this nation, then we of course could take appropriate remedies to deal with that situation. If on the other hand the evil exists, then it is our duty to place such appropriate restrictions on the individual liberty of those who are threatening our institutions by force as will ensure to the body politic that measure of liberty the maintenance of which is essential if our civilization is to be preserved.
There are those who say it would be a good thing if that civilization were done away with, and force is the only way it can be accomplished. That is what they said in Russia. Those who deify Lenin and those who follow in his footsteps say: Unfortunately you will find
there is only one way to deal with the situation, and that is by force. I recall the night that the report came out of the revolution in St. Petersburg. As I came out of the old museum building I happened to meet Sir Wilfrid Laurier and we stopped and discussed the matter for a moment. I pointed out that the last dispatches indicated that they had gone to the point of carving up the body of an-old admiral into cubes and dropping them under the ice as food for the fishes. I always remember the answer he gave. He said: Yes, these excesses are similar to what happened in the days of the French revolution; the very excesses will in themselves bring about the inevitable reaction. We now know that the excesses have brought about a reaction. But the period of time that elapsed between the commission of the offences against-shall I say, using a mild term-the amenities of civilization, and the day that the reaction began, was so prolonged that the effect upon the world as a whole has not yet been measured. I am not fearful at the moment that we are going to have an uprising in this country which will bring about by force similar results; not for a moment. Neither do I desire in any sense to magnify the possible result. But I do desire to point out as strongly as is within my power that unless we make some provision against such unlawful assemblies and those who constitute the membership in them we have not taken the steps to restrain individual activities and individual liberty that are essential to the maintenance of our national liberty. That in my judgment is quite clear.
Of course I am not unmindful of the argument that prevails in some quarters: "Let the commons repeal it; there is another chamber." But I am not impressed with that argument. The evidence of history is that after the commons house of parliament has acted in a matter five or six times, or after a government which has come fresh from the people with a great majority has passed certain legislation, neither in England nor on the continent or elsewhere has there ever been manifest a desire on the part of another chamber differently constituted as to views upon public issues to take action sharply different from that taken by the commons. There has always been in second chambers that recognition, which is sometimes designated by -harsh critics by another name, that recognition of the will of the people having asserted itself in a particular way, and the willingness to follow the pathway bla-zed by the commons.
I do not believe the Canadian people, if the question were submitted to them to-day by a plebiscite and they understood section
Criminal Code-Mr. Maclnnis

98, would desire to have it repealed. They would undoubtedly desire to have it modified, and I think along the lines I have suggested. I can do nothing with respect to the passage of this legislation. The government has announced that it proposes to repeal section 98. It has the power, and contends that it has the mandate to do so. I shall content myself with merely making this protest and asking the clerk at the table to record that the second reading of the bill was carried on division.

Mr. Speaker, before the bill is given
second reading I should like to say a few words. First of all may I say that from observations made this afternoon by hon. members to my right I am more and more convinced of the similarity between the Conservative and communist minds. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Wilton) could not understand anyone supporting views advocated by communists. He seems to forget that soviet Russia, the only country which has made any approach to the communist state-and of course it is not communist; they admit they are neither communist nor socialist-and the only country about which one thinks when he hears a reference to communism, was invited by the nations of the world, at a time when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was representing Canada, to participate in the activities of the League of Nations. That is clear proof that even a communist state or representative may have something of value to offer at this time.
Shortly after the leader of the opposition made his now famous radio talks prior to the session of 1936 I made a statement which appeared in the press to the effect that I was glad the then prime minister was going to do some of the things we had advocated for so many years. For that announcement a vote of censure came from communist sources. I believe it is time we departed from such childish attitudes of mind.
In connection with this legislation we of this group find ourselves in much the same position as we have been when other legislation has been before us. I am convinced that the present measure is an improvement, despite the language of section 4 of the bill, which I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will find his way to amend before final passage of the measure. The repeal of section 98 is desirable. People will have less difficulty in giving expression to their thoughts, even in regard to our so-called! institutions, without fear of being punished for so doing.

Beginning his observations the leader of the opposition said that the maintenance of liberty depends upon the restraint of individual liberty. That is true. To some extent the liberty of the mass depends upon the restraint of the liberty of the individual, and I am convinced that any government should, and must have sufficient powers to maintain order. But after I say that I must add that governments 'have functions in addition to that of the maintenance of order. [DOT]They m.ust find out why disorders arise, and must remove the cause not by repression but by making the necessary social and economic adjustments which will make disorder unnecessary. People do not become disorderly just for the mere joy of doing so. Of course some may, but I suggest the great majority do not. It is very difficult indeed to get people to act in an orderly fashion to remove an injustice in legal ways, let alone in a disorderly manner.
On various occasions in the debate reference has been 'made to Russia. That which* took place in Russia was the inevitable thing which would take place in any country governed as Russia was governed. The masses in Russia had no other recourse, no other possibility of making changes except through the use of force. I shall read briefly from the works of an author for whom I have great regard. Lord Macaulay, in his essay on Milton, dealing with the situation in England during the civil war of 1649 makes a case analogous to the situation in Russia in 1917. He writes:
Many evils, no doubt, were produced by the civil war. They were the price of our liberty.
Many evils undoubtedly followed the revolution in Russia, but is there anyone to-day who would want to put Russia back under the czars? There is not.
Has the acquisition been worth the sacrifice? It is the nature of the Devil of tyranny to tear and rend the body which he leaves. Are the miseries of continued possession less horrible than the struggles of the tremendous exorcism?
If it were possible that a people brought up under an intolerant and arbitrary system could subvert that system without acts of cruelty and folly, half the objections to despotic power would be removed. We should, in that case, be compelled to acknowledge that it at least produces no pernicious effects on the intellectual and moral character of a nation. We deplore the outrages which accompany revolutions. But the more violent the outrages, the more assured we feel that a revolution was necessary. The violence of those outrages will always be proportioned to the ferocity and ignorance of the pepole; and the ferocity and ignorance of the people will be proportioned to the oppression and degradation under which they have been accustomed

Criminal Code-Mr. Maclnnis
to live. Thus it was in our civil war. The heads of the church and state reaped only that which they had sown. The government had prohibited free discussion; it had done its best to keep the people unacquainted with their duties and their rights. The retribution was just and natural.
Is that not an accurate picture of the situation which maintained in Russia prior to the revolution of 1917? If in Canada we wish to make changes orderly, as they must be made, then we shall have to seek the causes of disorders, and not try to repress them by unwise laws. Lord Macaulay continues;
If our rulers suffered from popular ignorance, it was because they had themselves taken away the key of knowledge. If they were assailed with blind fury, it was because they had exacted an equally blind submission.
It is the character of such revolutions that we always see the worst of them at first. Till men have been sometime free, they know not how to use their freedom. The natives of wine countries are generally sober. In climates where wine is a rarity intemperance abounds.
And at a later point:
Ariosto tells a pretty story of a fairy, who, by some mysterious law of her nature, was condemned to appear at certain seasons in the form of a foul and poisonous snake. Those who injured her during the period of her disguise were forever excluded from participation in the blessings which she bestowed. But to those who, in spite of her loathsome aspect, pitied and protected her, she afterwards revealed herself in the beautiful and celestial form which was natural to her, accompanied their steps, granted all their wishes, filled their houses with wealth, made them happy in love and victorious in war. Such a spirit is liberty. At times she takes the form of a hateful reptile. She grovels, she hisses, she stings. But woe to those who in disgust shall venture to crush her! And happy are those who, having dared to receive her in her degraded and frightful shape, shall at length be rewarded by her in the time of her beauty and her glory!
I think it behooves hon. members to read those sentiments. In doing so they will realize that we can make progress only by continually seeking out the things that cause unrest. We have on our statute books a great many laws for the maintenance of order, but we have very few to prevent the exploitation of our people. We can make any law in this parliament bo maintain order, but let us try to make a law that seeks to prevent the exploitation of the masses of the people and immediately the question of its constitutionality is raised. Immediately it is taken to the courts.

There is obviously a distinction between the two types of statute. No one has ever questioned the competence of the dominion parliament to deal with criminal law, but when we consider the other
type of legislation to which the hon. member has referred, that is, social legislation, a considerable doubt as to competence has been entertained by the Department of Justice over a very long period of time.

That is the very point I wish to make. If this parliament had been intent on bringing about a better social organization, more economic equality and more social justice, then long ago it would have had the necessary constitutional authority to pass the necessary social legislation.
By consultation with the provinces.

By consultation with the provinces and by necessary changes in the constitution. Where there is a will there is a way, and these things can be done. What is the government going to do with the reform legislation passed last year which has been declared ultra vires? Is it going to let it go at that and say that nothing can be done about it? We will not get over these difficulties by increasing the military and police forces and building more penitentiaries. You can remove those conditions only by removing the social conditions which give them birth. I quote again from the same author:
There is only one cure for the evils which newly acquired freedom produces; and that cure is freedom. When a prisoner first leaves his cell he cannot bear the light of day; he is unable to discriminate colours, or recognize faces. But the remedy is, not to remand him into his dungeon, but to accustom him to the rays of the sun. The blaze of truth and liberty may at first dazzle and bewilder nations which have become half blind in the house of bondage. But let them gaze on, and they will soon be able to bear it. In a few years men learn to reason. The extreme violence of opinions subsides. Hostile theories correct each other. The scattered elements of truth cease to contend, and begin to coalesce. And at length a system of justice and order is educed out of the chaos.
Many politicians of our time-
This is about one hundred years ago, but the same is true to-day-
-are in the habit of laying it down as a self-evident proposition, that no people ought to be free till they are fit to use their freedom. The maxim is worthy of the fool in the old story, v7ho resolved not to go into the water till he had learnt to swim. If men are to wait for liberty till they become wise and good in slavery, they may indeed wait forever.
If men are to continue to live under the exploitation and misery which obtain under present economic conditions without making a protest, they will surely wait forever. It is only by protesting and by drawing attention
Criminal Code-Mr. Thorson

to these conditions that you can get. parliaments and governments to act.

There is no limitation on that right.
Mr. MaoINNIS: None whatsoever, but a person would almost think there was a limit because of how little of it has been done.
I do not want to occupy the time of the house in speaking further in this connection. I have not the necessary legal training with which to judge the value of the present bill. As I said in the beginning, I believe it is an improvement, but before the bill passes I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will find some way to define more clearly section 4. We will have so much accomplished, but it will not prevent our asking for more if more is necessary.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief in what I have to say. I support entirely the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when he introduced this measure. I should like also to commend the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) for the very moderate tone of his contribution to this debate. I am opposed to the retention of section 98 in our criminal code on two grounds. In the first place, I think it constitutes, if not directly then by implication, a threat to the right of free association. In the second place, I think it has been demonstrated through the course of time that this section is neither effective nor necessary for the safety of the state.
Our democratic system and our democratic institutions are under attack the world over, and it ought to be the duty of every person to maintain our existing democratic institutions so far as it is within his power to do so. The continued existence of these democratic institutions depends upon the maintenance of certain fundamental and precious rights. These are the rights of freedom of thought and speech, freedom of religion and freedom of association and assembly. These are the springs of progress and reform; they constitute the most precious heritage that we have derived from Great Britain, which has always been the home of individual liberty. In recent years we have seen the devastating results of the dictatorships that have been set up in various parts of the world, with their destruction of free institutions and their negation and denial of personal liberty. We must resist every encroachment upon every one of these fundamental rights.
I think we are all agreed that freedom of speech is essential to progress. New ideas are

necessary to reform. Our social system is far from perfect and we ought not to be too quick to find anything seditious or revolutionary in new ideas that may be advanced. Anyone who has read history knows that rebellion has often been the father of liberty, and that the rebel of yesterday is often the patriot of to-day. Indeed, the greatest reforms that have taken place have been the result of courageous attacks against existing institutions and what was then constituted authority. We ought to preserve in this chamber the right to criticize; we ought to preserve that right not only for ourselves but for every free citizen of this country, because freedom of opposition is essential to good government, just as essential as the government itself. Freedom of criticism outside this chamber is something that ought not to be curtailed in any way.
We have guaranteed freedom of religious thought and religious observance, and have gone a long way in this country to see that this great right is maintained. Yet there are people in Canada who would like to take away that right of religious freedom. Once you take away one right who can say when the next will disappear.
Perhaps the most valuable of the rights I have referred to is the right of free association, and it is because we feel that this right is threatened that we are opposed to the retention of section 98.

But the hon. gentleman
would say that it would have to be association for a lawful purpose, would he not?
Surely the hon. gentleman does not mean his statement just as he has said' it, -because that would mean unlawful associations. I think he must intend some limitation.

I would allow the right of association, and would not wish to see any interference with that right. If any member of an association is guilty of a breach of the peace, the law of sedition and the general law of the country relating to the preservation of the peace will be sufficiently wide to cover his particular case. There are certain rights that we possess, such as the right of free speech and free association, rights that are so valuable-
But free speech is limited.

Exactly. It is limited in the same way that the right of free association is limited when it comes to a question of the individual who breaks the law. The point I
wish to make is that reforms can come only as a result of organized effort, and we ought not to put any obstacle in the way of those who seek to associate with one another for the prosecution of necessary reforms. When it comes to breaches of the peace and questions affecting the safety of the state, we have ample legislation to ensure our interests in that regard. I shall deal with that aspect of the matter in a moment.
I think it will be generally agreed that, so far as this subject is concerned, this is the mildiest debate that has taken place in this house and that speakers throughout the debate have adopted a more moderate tone than in similar previous discussions. This legislation has passed the House of Commons, I believe, six times, and been rejected by the Senate. On a number of occasions in former debates the opposition to the repeal of section 98 was based upon the ground that the section had never been used and that, therefore, there was no harm in its retention. But it has recently been used.
In the course of this debate a good deal has been said about communism, and I should like to add a few words on the subject. In my opinion communism in this country is a bogey. I do not believe we need have any fear of it if we insist upon the maintenance of our individual rights and liberties. I also suggest that communism will never be put down by what may be described as the iron heel of ruthlessness; any attempt to suppress communism by force will strengthen communistic activities rather than weaken them, for martyrdom begets sympathy and it creates followers; that has been the history of such movements in the past and it has been our experience in recent years. The most effective course to follow in our combat with communism and the best weapon we can use is to remove the causes of discontent, for communistic leaders feed their followers upon discontent. The next best course is to bring communism right out into the open. I say to the right hon. leader of the opposition that the release of the communist leaders on parole was a more effective step towards the diminution of communistic strength than was their arrest and conviction. When they were arrested and convicted, the effect was to drive their activities underground. When they were released and were free to appear on every platform as leaders of communism, the people had an opportunity of listening to them and their activities were brought out into the open. We know the result at the last election. They had, I believe, eleven candidates in the field in the dominion. Nearly
392S
Criminal Code-Mr. Thorson

all of them lost their deposits; many of them got very few votes. I recall my own experience in meeting communistic activity in the constituency which I now represent. At the end of my speeches we had question time. At that time the communist agents were there; they followed me from place to place, particularly in those polls which had been strongly communistic. The people enjoyed immensely the questions and the answers that were given those questions. In polls where communistic activity had been strong, so strong in 1930 that the votes in such polls were almost solidly communistic, the people had been listening to communistic propaganda for the past five years, had heard the promises made by the communist leaders, had been examining what had been placed before them by the communists. At the last election support of communism almost disappeared, or if it did not disappear, it dwindled in many cases to negligible proportions. I think that indicates the best course to follow.
In my opinion the right hon. leader of the opposition made the best argument in support of the repeal of section 98 that could possibly be made when he said that the provincial authorities had refused to enforce it. The reason they did so is, no doubt, that public opinion was against the enforcement of the legislation. When a statute reaches the point where it no longer holds the support and approval of public opinion the time has come for its repeal.
Particular use has been made of the bogey of communism to frighten the people of Canada against the activities of communists, particularly in districts where the people are of foreign origin. While I am speaking on this subject I desire to say a few words on behalf of one class of foreign-born Canadians, the Ukrainians. There is a good1 deal of communistic activity among the Ukrainian people of this country, but nowhere is there fiercer opposition to the progress of communism than among the Ukrainian people. Their organizations are fighting it ceaselessly and are carrying on against it a more intense drive than anj'one else. It is out in the open; in my opinion, there is no need to fear in the least the progress of communism so long as we maintain and insist upon our full rights of individual liberty and freedom. I would also point out that the main leaders of communistic activity in this dominion are not of foreign origin; they are of English or Scottish origin.
The danger of communism has been magnified particularly in the province of Quebec, where the Liberal party has been pictured as

though it wyere in league with communism. Nothing could be farther from the truth. Nothing could be falser than the cartoon on this subject which was published widely in the province of Quebec, portraying the Liberal party as being the friend and the ally of communism. The principles of Liberalism are fundamentally different from those of communism.

On this subject, sir, I wish to say a few words in French to my friends from the province of Quebec. They know that the great principle of Liberalism is individual liberty and that the Liberal party will safeguard the rights they hold sacred. The hon. members from the province of Quebec, whose speeches in this house I have listened to with pleasure, express themselves sometimes in French and sometimes in English. But when using the French language, they too often create the impression that the right to speak French in this house is the exclusive privilege of Canadians of French origin. I feel that I should protest against that claim because this right belongs to every hon. member of this house irrespective of his origin.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

This is the first time that I venture to address this house in French, but, sir, when I endeavour to do so, I exercise a right which is as much mine as yours.
What are our most valuable rights? I think you will agree with me that they are freedom of speech, liberty of creed, and the right of free association. My hon. friends the members from the province of Quebec will allow me to tell them one thing: If you tolerate any encroachment on these rights, even on that of free association as was done in section 98 of the criminal code, the door will be wide open to attacks against other rights which you prize even more dearly. Who could then tell where such encroachments would stop? If you are careful to safeguard all individual rights, you will have no cause to fear the inroads of communism.
(Text) We are in even greater danger in this country, Mr. Chairman, of falling into fascism than of being overcome by communism. There may be some value in the philosophy underlying some of the teachings of communism, much as we may be opposed to the manner in which communism was sought to be established in Russia, but I can see no value in the fundamental philosophy of fascism. Men give up the struggle for democratic government when they lose faith in themselves. It is then that they want action. It is then that they demand strong men to carry on

Criminal Code
government. It is then that they are prepared to surrender their personal liberties. When men have reached that stage they are in a state of despair. I do not believe there is any need for despair. I believe that under our democratic system of government we can bring about necessary reforms if we give proper attention to them and if we allow full and free play to the force that we should derive from the full exercise of our rights of free speech, freedom of assembly and freedom of association.
We have now had section 98 in the criminal code for some seventeen years. The provincial authorities have ceased to enforce this section. Labour organizations are opposed to its retention. There are serious defects in many of the details of the section. It has not proved an effective means of combatting the advance of communism. It will not be an effective means of combatting the advance of fascism, nor is it necessary for the preservation of the state. We have ample other legislation for the purpose. If any member of any association or organization is guilty of endangering the state the general law is wide enough. Certain offences against the state are provided for by the law of treason. The general law of sedition is as wide as it is safe for such a law to be. It is elastic; its application depends upon circumstances. We have sedition generally; we have seditious libel and seditious conspiracy, all designed for certain circumstances and certain occasions. We have laws against riots, riotous assembly and unlawful assembly. I would say that the legislation we already have is quite sufficient for the preservation of the state without making any unnecessary encroachment upon fundamental rights which are essential to progress and reform.
For this reason, and for the reasons I have already mentioned, I feel that section 98 constitutes an unwarranted interference with the right of free association; that it has not been effective in accomplishing its purpose and that it is not necessary for the preservation of the state. I am very glad indeed to support the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in everything he said, and will support the second reading of this bill.
