speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In order to clarify the language, as well as the meaning, of this section, I would add the words "within Canada" at the end of the section, which then would Tend, "any governmental change within Canada." I have found that in the United' States that is the wording used, "against the government of the United States."

It will be recalled that the original section of the act provided for a case where efforts were made to destroy the oonstitued government of the united kingdom, or of Canada, or of any of the provinces. "Within Canada" is not quite as broad sis that provision of the section, which was generally accepted1 as not being an unfair provision as far as that phase was concerned.

Would this not very much
weaken the possibility of conviction? All that would be needed would be for the seditious language to be in general terms; then the accused could plead: Oh, I was referring to any governmental change not in Canada, but in some other country. As long as he used such words as "overthrow the government," that is all right, so long as he did not say "overthrow the government of Canada." Even if the language used' were related: to a neighbouring friendly state I do not know whether we particularly want to give shelter to those who, perhaps just within the border, want to carry on an extensive propaganda against the government of a neighbouring state. But I particularly call the attention of the minister to this point; as long as they couch their seditious utterances in general languge could they not plead that this section did not apply, if it contains the words "within Canada"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The
language used will certainly serve to interpret the meaning. I really believe it is 'better to restrict the section in that way. If somebody talks about Haiti or some other country in

Criminal Code

distant parts of the world where there may be trouble, I do not see why our law should' make that a crime. And as I said, the legislation, of other countries contains a similar limitation; they restrict the scope of the provision to their own country.

The section I had' in
mind is section 133A:
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in goor faith-
(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the United Kingdom, or of any part of it, or of Canada or any province thereof, or in either house of
arliament of the United Kingdom or of
anada, or in any legislature, or in the administration of justice; or to excite His Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in the state; or
(c)	to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing or have a tendency to produce feelings of hatred and illwill between different classes of His Majesty's subjects.
I think there is a point to what the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) has said. It seems to me, having regard to our geographical position, that we are making matters a title difficult, if we have some of the highly skilled persons with whom I came into contact during the last few years in dealing with the question. I shall not mention names, but they will say: Oh, I was not saying a word about Canada; I had not the slightest intention of saying anything about Canada; I am just saying that this is a rotten way to govern a country. That is exactly what they will do.

For many years England was an asylum for political refugees, from Italy, Austria, and was even used as a base from which they carried on their political propaganda. They were welcomed even by ministers of the government. For example, if anybody thought that Haile Selassie had been improperly put out of his kingdom I do not know why there might not be some people in this country or in England who might do something to assist in restoring him to his throne. I assume .the Italians are now the de facto government of Ethiopia. I think the united kingdom can look after itself without our worrying about what some might say about what might happen in Great Britain, and as for the country near by, I was reading just a little while ago that book of Sinclair Lewis's, It Can't Happen Here. Some may recall that the nazi people, or some acting very much along nazi lines, are portrayed as having set up a gouvermment in
,Mr. E. Lapointe.]
the United States. In that story Canada is represented as being an asylum for those seeking to get away from the outrages that prevailed in the United States. If anything of that kind happened I do not know but what a good many of us would welcome such refugees, and it might be difficult to prevent them from carrying on political propaganda. Surely the whole purpose is to protect anything that may need protection here in Canada. As I said this morning, as the clause now stands it would mean that we would have to rule out of our libraries a great part of the histories now found there. It would mean that all except convinced pacifists would have a great deal of difficulty in expressing their opinions as to the possibilities of force.

I think that is hardly a correct statement. But is there not some international law that creates an obligation upon us in this regard? The minister will no doubt recall that when there was organized in London a conspiracy against Napoleon III, considerable discussion arose, and it crosses my mind that the general rule of international law among friendly peoples is that those who are agitating against the destruction of an existing form of government in other countries shall not find opportunity to carry forward such propaganda in a friendly country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is another section of the code which relates to offences against foreign sovereigns. There is a provision relating to His Majesty the King and his countries or dominions; there are sections 78, 79, 80 and 81. There is a section somewhere that makes it an offence to use offensive language towards sovereigns of other nations. But what I rise to say is that if we have nothing in tthe criminal code, the ordinary law would apply with regard to sedition. As the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said this morning, anything -under the common law which is not repugnant to any statute of Canada applies in this country. Everything which, under the common law, relates to seditious offences in Great Britain, applies to Canada, except when we have something which would be repugnant to it. I do not believe that this amendment was necessary at all, except to make the section clearer. As we say in the section, the provision has not the effect of limiting the generality of the meaning of the expression "seditious intention." Anything that is seditious outside this provision continues to be seditious. But when the offence is that of circulating or printing a

Criminal Code
document in which is advocated the use of force as a means to accomplish governmental change in Canada, we have a special offence for which provision is made in the amendment before us. But it has not the effect of taking away other seditious offences. For instance, reference was made to provincial legislatures. The provision in that regard will still exist. May I call the attention of the committee to the fact that in section 98, which is being repealed, the words "within Canada" are used. I want to repeal section 98, but I do not wish to 'replace it by something which will be more strict.

I believe the addition of the words "within Canada" serve to clarify and carry out the law. The criminal code expressly states that where we have not legislated by parliamentary enactment. the law of England as it stands to-day and as it stood at that time applies. If there # are any omissions in a statute we still have the common law of England to fall back upon. It is my opinion that cases of sedition will not be tried before county magistrates as was suggested by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. They will be tried in courts before trained judges.
I did not say "tried"; I used the word "investigated."

There are other provisions in the criminal code which cover what should be our friendly relations with other countries. I do not think it is competent for us to legislate what is sedition in another country. In fact, I cannot recall the name of the case-if I had the memory of the leader of the opposition, I might do so-but I cited it within the year, and I remember that it dealt with a distinguished Frenchman who was tried in England for uttering seditious language against-
Napoleon III.

' The Frenchman was acquitted because it was held that he had the right of free speech in England. In defending him his counsel said, on behalf of the prisoner, that one of the greatest sights injured innocence could see was the prisoner in the box looking upon twelve jurymen of his country, of Which country they were for that trial. Right nobly they maintained that tradition and the man was acquitted.
I believe the section covers all any person could ask for by way of protection against seditious utterances calculated to overthrow the government of Canada. One argument was made to the effect that by repealing
section 98 we were weakening our law and offering an invitation to evilly disposed people to continue preaching seditious doctrines. May I remind those who make that argument that our law, even section 98, does not begin to compare with the law as it stood in Russia in 1917 or in France before the revolution. The laws of neither country, harsh as they were, in the slightest degree prevented the revolutions; on the contrary I believe they contributed largely to bringing them about.
Amendment agreed to..

Would not the Minister of
Justice be good enough to try even to a limited degree to give us some idea of what he means by the use of the words "everyone shall be presumed to have a seditious intention." This expression is causing a great deal of perturbation and even lawyers who have read it believe it could be interpreted widely. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to
the first point raised may I say that in any prosecution it will be the duty of the prosecutor first to prove an overt act. The prosecutor will have to prove that the accused person has published or circulated a writing or document in which force is advocated, or that by words that person has incited the use of force. When this is done the seditious intention is presumed. Perhaps the wording might have been different, but first of all there will have to be proof that the accused person has advocated the use of force; he is not presumed to be guilty of having advocated force, until that has been proved. When such proof is offered, seditious intention will be presumed from the fact that he has committed the act. That places a different complexion upon the objection of the hon. member.
I know what the hon. member has in mind in connection with the second point he raises. My right hon. friend referred to a legal opinion offered by counsel for the labour organization, in which it was stated that the.
Criminal Code

word "force" in section 98 might be interpreted as other than physical force. For instance, in strikes there would be picketing and that sort of thing. The reason this particular counsel held that opinion was that after the Winnipeg strike Mr. Justice Metcalfe said the prisoner had stated that he wanted to use force to obtain redress for labour, and that he was referring to the moral force employed by the labour organization during the strike. Surely that would not apply in this section; this applies only to governmental changes. The word "force" as it appears in this section means physical force only.

Would the minister
indicate whether the words "publishes or circulates" would apply to a person who sells the article?

Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Kootenay East) moved the second reading of Bill No. 108, to enable the establishment, operation and maintenance of free foreign trade zones.
He said:	This 'bill was introduced in the
other chamber. The only reason I mention that is to shorten my own remarks, by saying that it was before a committee of the senate that examined into the matter very carefully and reported it unanimously, and' it was forwarded to this house in due course.
A brief statement of the bill is to this effect, that it authorizes the government by licence to permit provinces, municipalities, or public agencies to establish in any suitable port of Canada what is known as a free port zone. Some had the idea that a free port meant a port free of charges. That, of course, is not correct at all. It simply means an area within a port where goods may be received without entry through customs and may there be reprocessed, manufactured oU-o-od jn any
Criminal Code

way and resKipped by export or admitted to the country under the usual customs regulations. I suppose the most outstanding free port in the world is that of Hamburg. Many others have been established in various parts of the world. I believe it was nearly twenty-five years ago that I personally brought this question up in the house and on several occasions during the next ten years I suggested or urged the establishment of free port zones in Canada, but parliament prior to some years ago had not seen fit to approve. However the idea or the policy of free port zones has considerably progressed since those days, and there are many such zones established in various countries of the world, detailed information regarding which may be foundi in the printed evidence of the senate committee which has been distributed to all members of the house. The bill does not impose any charge on the state. It is a permissive measure authorizing the government to license these public agencies to establish such a free port zone if, when and as the government may decide. As section 19 of the bill reads:
No provision of this act shall be read as imposing or intending to impose, directly, indirectly or consequentially, upon His Majesty or upon the public revenues of Canada any expenditure or expense-

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
This bill is a very important measure; it has come to the House of Commons at a late stage in the session, and the government has not had an opportunity of considering it in all its implications. I have read the bill, and I have read some of the representations-very strong representations-made against the bill to the senate committee that considered it, but I do not propose to go to-night into the subject of its merits. It has manifestly come to us at so late a stage that we cannot consider it as we should consider a bill of this importance. I therefore, Mr. Speaker, beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 96, to amend the criminal code-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
At six o'clock I was saying a few words about section 9.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am in the judgment of the committee, but my recollection is that section 9 was passed and that we were at section 10.
No, Mr. Chairman. At six o'clock I was speaking on section 9. It could not have been carried. I was speaking when you rose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is a mistake; the section carried; but I should be quite willing to let my hon. friend go back to section 9.
On section 9-Motor cars.

I do not wish to be unfair. I am trying to put this bill through. Later on I propose to help the house a little to hurry along. I think this section is an improvement, but I hope that in the recess of parliament the minister will consider the position of first offenders in the matter of what I was referring to at six o'clock as joy-riding. I mentioned the case of three young people belonging to a baseball team. They took out for two or three hours the car of a gentleman who was connected with them, and on coming back they were arrested; under the present law they are liable to imprisonment for a year. They have never been in any trouble before. I suggest that during the recess of parliament this motor car question should be referred to the law officers of the crown and something done to take care of matters of this kind. I believe this bill should have come down in the early days of the session, because it is a law reform affecting the most important thing we have, the liberty of the subject. In the dying days of the session many of the lawyers have gone home, and this bill does not get the consideration it should. I hope in the recess the minister will look into the matter carefully.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have much sympathy with those who want to enjoy themselves in the way my hon. friend suggests, but if this section is not amended as provided in this bill those young people who, without any right, take motor cars for the purpose of joy-riding are liable to be charged with theft, which carries a much heavier penalty. On the whole I think it is better to make the amendment.

Section agreed to.

Possession of instruments of disguise.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have an amendment, inserting the word "vaultbreaking" after the word "housebreaking" in line 27.

Criminal Code

I move accordingly.
Section as amended agreed to.
Sections 11 to 20 inclusive agreed to.
On section 21-Defence of insanity.

Is there not still a six man jury in Alberta? The number in Manitoba and Saskatchewan was reduced to six, and if the Alberta jury is still six in number I think that province should be mentioned also.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know the law has been changed as far as Saskatchewan and Manitoba are concerned, but I could not say as to Alberta.
I am told that the number is still six in Alberta, so I think we had better add that province also.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am advised that there has been no change in Alberta.

Then Alberta should be included also, if there is a six man jury there. This question of the sanity or insanity of an accused who sets up the plea of insanity under the old section of the code was decided by a jury of twelve, which is the usual number. But if Alberta still has a jury of six this section should read, "or in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta or Manitoba by any six jurors." Otherwise you would leave Alberta with the twelve jurors trying an issue of insanity while in that province there is no provision for more than six jurors.

In Alberta all juries are and have been composed of six men. This amendment provides that if there is an insanity issue directed before the trial proceeds, it shall be tried by twelve jurors except in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. If you do not specifically include Alberta in this section it will, I think, be found that the insanity issue will have to be tried by twelve jurors in Alberta, because this is a special provision for the trial of an insanity issue before the accused is given in charge to a jury. Of course, after he is given in charge on the main issue, there would be no necessity for mentioning Alberta, because they have always had juries of six in that province. That point of course is covered elsewhere.
As far as I am concerned I should like to see twelve jurors try these issues in all provinces. I do not want to hold up the committee but I am very much against six man juries in criminal cases. Of course, if you are going to have a six man jury try the main
issue, I suppose it is logical to have a six man jury try the insanity issue as well, but I think many lawyers in Saskatchewan and Manitoba now agree that the twelve man jury is the right jury to try people, charged with serious crimes, rather than a six man jury which really is not a jury at all under English law.

The other day the
appellate division of the Supreme Court of Manitoba decided that a six man jury was valid.

Yes, because the parliament of Canada had enacted that a six man jury should try cases in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. As far as I am concerned, however-and I think many lawyers in Saskatchewan would agree-a six man jury never should have been established for criminal cases. Most lawyers held the opinion that it was quite all right to establish six man juries for civil cases, but when this was done that was used as the basis for asking that a six man jury should be established for criminal cases. I believe the experience has been that when you cut your jury from twelve to six the tendency is towards trial by judge and no longer trial by judge and jury, because six men are more readily subject to the influence of the opinion of the judge. It will soon be commonly urged that since you have got down to six man juries the next step should be to do away with juries altogether and have trial by three judges sitting together. Personally I see no reason why, when citizens accused of a crime in the rest of Canada can demand that they shall not be found guilty	except by	a jury of	twelve men,	wein the	west when	so accused	should be in	theposition of being liable to be found guilty by six men. Anyone can see that the chances of being found guilty unanimously, as must be the case in criminal matters, by a six man jury are practically double the chances of being found guilty by a twelve man jury. Ever	since the	beginning	of Anglo-Saxonjurisprudence the jury has been composed of twelve men, and personally I should like to see that practice brought back. I do not agree	with the	six man	jury system	for
criminal cases. I hope the Minister of Justice will secure the opinions of some of the organized legal bodies in Saskatchewan and Manitoba during the next year or so, and I think he will find that the opinion of most lawyers is that in criminal cases we should go back to the twelve man jury.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that this change, which was made under the former administration, was brought about
Criminal Code

at the request of the provincial authorities of both Saskatchewan and Manitoba. As far as Alberta is concerned, under the Alberta Act that province had the right to keep the jury procedure as it was in the old Northwest Territories, and that is still the case, so it does not come under the present section.

But will it not come under the present section?
As it is now it covers all Canada except Manitoba and Saskatchewan, in terms which are exact and precise:
If such issue is directed before the accused is given in charge to a jury for trial on the indictment, such issue shall be tried by any twelve jurors, or in the provinces of Saskatchewan or Manitoba by any six jurors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course it was the same drafting before, and still Alberta was under special laws. But my right hon. friend is right when he says that as the section appears the whole of Canada except Manitoba and Saskatchewan would require twelve jurors. I am told by my officer that Alberta does not come under this section at all.
I do not know how it is possible to legislate for all Canada and leave out one province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe that all the provinces which are excepted could be named in this section. However I shall take that into consideration, and possibly next year we shall do as we have done this year, correct these little anomalies as they appear. We have corrected many this year, and I know some still remain. This appears to be one.

I do not want to delay the work of the committee, but I find it difficult to accommodate myself to this. Here is a section which reads as I have indicated; when a plea of insanity is set up, as seldom arises, the law of Alberta says there shall be six jurors. Counsel will say: No, it is provided by section 21 of a federal statute passed in 1936 that except in Saskatchewan and Manitoba the number shall be twelve.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I agree with my right hon. friend that it seems anomalous.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 21 carry?
No; it is either right or wrong. The minister says he agrees with me. Let us include Alberta; that is the short way to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid it will necessitate other changes. Alberta is dealt with-
Yes, under the Northwest Territories Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It looks strange but that is the position as it exists. If we change it, there may be no bad effect, but I would rather postpone this clause and see whether the matter could be dealt with in the way my right hon. friend suggests without interfering with some other clause.
Ear be it from me to stand in the way of a minister of the crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall undertake to see whether this can be done, and, if so, have it done by the senate.

Section agreed to.
Section 22 agreed to.
On section 23-Commencement of act.
Why the delay?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed that it is the usual practice to give notice to the various provinces of amendments to the criminal code.

Before the committee
passes the bill I have the consent of the Minister of Justice to bring up an amendment. The amendments are set out in Bills Nos. 5 and 57. I did not discuss this on second reading because there was so much discussion. But these are two of the most important bills dealt with this session. The minister promised me that the bill would be given consideration and in the committee I could add Bills Nos. 5 and 57. Owing to the length of the session I do not wish to delay the committee more than four or five minutes.
Bill No. 57 relates to motor cars. We have spent considerable time discussing one clause of an act which concerns only eight or nine people in Canada, and here is Bill No. 57 which concerns the lives of nine thousand people who will be killed and of more thousands wounded, yet we stand still and do nothing. I would urge consideration of this bill. I do not believe many hon. members have ever seen it. The bill did not get the consideration it should have had. It relates to level crossings, driving under the influence of liquor; it proposes to stop racing and cutting in; it provides that a person having caused death shall not drive for two years, and for women jurors on the trial of a woman accused, and it deals with cases where a charge of manslaughter arises out of the operation of a motor vehicle, providing that there may be

Criminal Code
a conviction for culpable negligence, a jury to decide whether the accused is guilty or not guilty.
The other bill had to do with giving people time to pay fines. I propose to substitute for the present law the law of England, known as "time to pay.'-
I am not asking the committee to adopt these bills to-night, but I say that the country from coast to coast is crying out to this parliament to stop this slaughter on the highways. It is one of the crimes of this age. Some of us here may be knocked down by a motor car and not be able to come back next session. Transportation should be the means to an end, and not an end in itself. What I suggested early in the session was that we should have real law reform in this country. Constitutional, parliamentary, cabinet and law reform are among the most important matters before us. The minister told me that he would not oppose it if I added some of these amendments to the bill. He was most sympathetic in regard to this question. I ask him if he will be kind enough during the recess to have his law officers look into this question of death on the highway. Hundreds of thousands of people are killed every year all over the world. They do not get a chance; they are just sent to eternity in five seconds. Our law is away behind the times; it was made about the time the motor car came into use. The minister requested me to let the bill stand. Some hon. members want to discuss the bill.
If no action is taken this session I am going to continue to press this bill and I hope at the opening of next session a committee of both houses of parliament, as was the case in England, will be appointed to take up this question of law reform, death and accidents by motor cars, the terrible toll of life and the question of the level crossings, and bring the law up to date. In England by taking action they have reduced these accidents fifty per cent. I admit that this matter is partly in the control of the provinces, but the criminal law is federal. Some people driving motor cars are not fit to drive them. In these days a motor car or a motor truck is a death dealing instrument in the hands of those who do not know how to handle it. As evidence of that fact we need only read the lists of week end fatalities during the summer months. We could fill these 245 seats five times over with the people badly injured since the first of January in the city from which I come, and of that number there were twenty-four deaths.
I am asking the minister to give this matter careful consideration; he has promised to do that. I would ask that it be considered early in the next session and that a committee of
both houses be appointed to see if we cannot get some relief from the great numbers of tragedies on our highways. Dear knows we are far enough behind the times as it is, and while I do not want to press the matter at this time-I would like to see prorogation come quickly; the house cannot close quickly enough for me-I should like to see something done. The minister told me that if I withdrew Bill No. 5 he would give it consideration. I am asking him to do so, because I do not want to see him knocked down, and in view of the speed with which motor cars pass this building it is possible that he could be. I would like to see him five a good many more years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as Bill No. 5 is concerned may I tell the hon. member I have communicated with the attorneys general of the provinces. Six of them have replied, and generally may I say that they are not in agreement with the delayed payment of fines suggested by the hon. member. Under section 739 of the criminal code, which deals with summary convictions, under the law magistrates have the discretion to allow a limited time for the payment of fines. That provision may be sufficient to meet most of the cases the hon. member has in mind. However I am prepared to give the matter full consideration during the recess and to discuss it again with him at the next session.
The other bill to which he has referred deals with an important matter, and it too will be fully considered. The hon. member would make it an offence to cross railway tracks without first having come to a stop, and having started again in low gear. There are many objections to the proposal. We have received strong objections from almost every automobile association including the Manitoba Motor League, the Canadian Automobile Association, the Hamilton Automobile Club and the Nova Scotia Motor League. They state that the provision would be unfair to motorists, particularly to visiting tourists, and would be impossible of enforcement. They claim, too, that the danger would be increased, because after starting their engines in low gear the motorists might have a tendency to stall their motors in the middle of railway tracks. However, it is a fact that in my own province of Quebec this is one of the traffic regulations, although it may not always be observed by motorists. I would hesitate at this time, however, to make it an offence not to abide by such a regulation.
The other proposal of the hon. member is to make it an offence for a driver to operate
Criminal Code

his motor car while under the influence of alcohol. The present law states that he shall not do so "while intoxicated." This proposal would involve an important change and would also involve difficulties in connection with the interpretation of the expression "while under the influence of liquor." If, by some magistrates, a man who has had one drink were ruled to be under the influence of liquor, such a law would be dangerous. Of course, when prohibition was in force in Canada conditions might have been different, but in these days the liquor traffic is legal, and one drink taken by a man who drives his car should not, according to the judgment of many, be considered a crime. I do not know whether my hon. friend has a chauffeur, but if such a law were enforced those people who can afford the services of a chauffeur would be in a better position than the poorer people who cannot afford chauffeurs and would have to abstain altogether from having even a drink of beer, when in charge of their motor cars. I believe it would be well to give this matter more consideration, and again I promise the hon. member that I shall be pleased to do so.
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the title carry?

I beg
the indulgence of the committee to revert to section 19. I am sorry I did not notice how drastic it was when it was passed.
You are too late.

Perhaps I am; but there are some lawyers in the house who will be kicking themselves when they go home if some change is not made. I refer to the fact- that by section 19 it is made obligatory upon a person committed fourteen days before the sitting of the court to make his election within ten days of that sitting as to whether he is to be tried by a jury. I think that is a provision which is entirely too drastic in its scope and effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This
change has been requested by eminent legal authorities in various provinces, and more particularly by the Attorney General of Nova Scotia. It is for the purpose of avoiding heavy expenditures by the crown and to compel the crown to summon witnesses and to submit the case to the grand jury. When a true bill is found the accused elects whether he will go before the district judge rather than before a jury. I think on the whole the change commends itself because the

accused person will have all the time necessary to make his election, and the crown will not be compelled to incur heavy expenditures.

Might this also apply
to a case where a person might elect for trial by a magistrate under part XVI of the code? Would he have to elect within the time specified in this measure? I have not had time to look the matter up. Can the minister tell me whether a person desiring to be tried by a magistrate under part XVI would be required to elect within the time specified in this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; that would not apply; it would apply only to those who are on bail.
Who are committed.

A provincial magistrate
in Saskatchewan can try any case a district court or county court judge can try. I would like to know whether this would require an election ten days ahead in cases where prisoners desired to be tried by a magistrate, under part XVI.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A man
has to be committed or sent for trial.

After a person has had a preliminary inquiry in Saskatchewan and is committed for trial, he can then elect to be tried by a district court judge or by a magistrate under part XVI. I would like to know whether he must elect within the time specified in this section if he wishes to be tried by a magistrate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This applies only to a case that comes before a jury. He has to make an election to go before a jury or to 'be tried by either a magistrate or a district court judge.

Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

Mr. Speaker, I beg to move:
That a message be sent to the senate acquainting their honours that this house disagrees with their amendments to Bill No. 17, an act respecting the National Harbours Board, for the following reasons:
1.	Amendment 1 makes impossible reemployment of many officers and employees of present harbour boards who have long years of service, and in addition would seriously handicap the board in the conduct of its many competitive business operations.
2.	Amendment 2 arises out of amendment 1, and is not otherwise required.
3.	Amendment 3 proposes restrictions that serve no useful purpose and which are not presently imposed on other government services.
4.	Amendment 5 is permissive only and confers on the board no new authority. The government holds the view that the step specified by this clause is not desirable at this moment.

1.	That with the exception of clause A, the amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 67, an act to amend the Customs Act be concurred in.

subtopic: NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
There are fifteen amendments made by the senate, most of which are very minor; but a few are of some importance. I move:
That a message be sent to the senate to acquaint their honours that this house agrees to their fifth, sixth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth and fourteenth amendments to Bill No. 75, an act to amend the Income War Tax Act, and disagrees to their first, second, third, fourth, seventh, eighth and ninth amendments for the following reasons:-
Because, respecting the first amendment, paragraphs C and D of the first schedule of the act are "enacted" by section two of chapter forty of the statutes of 1935, not reenacted. To "reenact" is to enact again in the same terms. These paragraphs were enacted by the act of 1935 in terms different from that of the repealed paragraphs.
Because, respecting the second amendment, the first schedule of the act is repealed in precise words by the act of 1932-33, and a new schedule "enacted." The schedule is, therefore, not "amended."
Broadcasting Corporation

Because, respecting the third, fourth, eighth and ninth amendments, the reasons for disagreeing to the second amendment apply equally to these amendments, and further, because these changes would have the effect of substituting a new and incorrect method of drafting the enacting words in a clause of a bill, a method contrary to that which has constantly been followed up to the present time, and would further have the effect of disrupting the uniformity of our statutes.
Because, respecting the seventh amendment, the word "and" would be substituted for the word "or," which is already in the act, and the effect would be contrary to the desired intention of the section, which is that a company shall be liable for the tax "if it should fail to file the annual return or to pay the said filing fee," that is, the company shall be liable in either case.
And further, that this house, with respect to the fifteenth amendment made by the senate agree to their amendment with an amendment to their amendment as follows:-
For the words "of said subsection (8)" substitute the words "of this subsection," for the reason that the words "of said subsection (8)" would be part of subsection (8) itself. As the words are incorporated in the subsection, it is preferable to use the words "of this subsection"; and

that as far as the Yukon is concerned the radio is almost entirely worthless. subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL BROADCASTING SERVICE AND REPEAL OF ACT OF 1932
speechtext:
Why is it thought desirable that this corporation shall be solely under the control of the government? We had hoped that broadcasting in Canada might be out of the hands of governments. An effort was made in that direction; indeed, I think it was an accomplished fact, and the commission acted without considering the political effects of its conduct. Section 9 states that the corporation shall not enter into any negotiations without the consent in writing of the minister. subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO FEES, CHARGES AND ROYALTIES, AND TO CONSTITUTE A COPYRIGHT APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
I do not intend to deal at any great length with the bill, which has already been referred to on two different occasions during the course of the session. I merely wish to remind the committee that this bill deals solely with performing rights of musical compositions. In practice the different sections of the bill are consequent upon the inquiry conducted by Judge Parker, appointed by the former government to inquire into the business of the Canadian Performing Right Society.
The act of 1931 provided for a commissioner to make an inquiry into the fees charged by a society, holding a number of copyrights. The inquiry took place in 1935 and the report was handed to the government during October of that year.
By an additional bill also introduced by the former government in 1935 a stay of proceedings while the inquiry was going on, was enacted, and inasmuch as the legislation was made necessary to allow this government to give effect to the inquiry conducted by Judge Parker, therefore the stay of proceedings has been continued ever since. It is absolutely urgent that this parliament at this session give the Secretary of State, who is in charge of copyright, the proper authority to give effect to some of the proposals made by the commissioner.
The report, which I have tabled and which I am sure is in the hands of everyone interested in the bill, made several recommendations. I just want to point them out in the order in which they appear in the bill.
The first section deals with a definition of private profit. The second section deals with the filing of appeals and the appointment of an appeal board. Then a subsection is introduced to prevent factious and unwarranted legal proceedings, also the recommendation of the judge. The last two subsections give the Secretary of State authority to make an adjustment of fees from January, 1935, when the tariff of fees was filed by the performing right society, until the date the appeal board which is proposed to be instituted makes its first report. I do not wish at present to say any more, but come to the first clause which is for the consideration of the committee. This is as recommended by Judge Parker, a clearer and more complete definition of what constitutes a performance without private profit. In the act of 1931 it was provided that no infringement of copyright could take place in a performance without private profit, one for religious, educational or charitable purposes. In another subsection it was pro-
Copyright Amendment Act
vided that that should also include any agricultural exhibition or fair held under dominion, provincial or municipal authority. It is proposed in this first section of the present bill to make a clearer definition of what is a performance without private profit.
I now draw the attention of the committee to the first subsection of section 1, the underlined words:
Provided, further, that such performance shall be deemed to be given without private profit if the only fees which are paid are paid to individual performers and that no fees or commissions are paid to any promoter, producer or contractor for services in promoting or producing the performance.
That is concerning performances for religious, educational or charitable purposes. I want to make it very clear that we are not now proposing the principle that the performer might be paid while the owner of the copyright might not be paid. The question is that we are dealing with the small rights of performers. It often happens that in a charitable concert, or performances of a certain kind, you may have most of the performers performing gratuitously, but if there happens to be a performer who receives a consideration for his work then in cases which have appeared before the court some judges have had doubt as to the meaning of the legislation. It was also the opinion of the judge who held the inquiry that the intention of the legislation in 1931 in defining private profit regarded the profit of the performance as a whole, and not that of the individual performer.
As to the second subsection, dealing with agricultural exhibitions, we propose a similar definition. I must say that on that subsection hon. members from all provinces and from all directions have come to me suggesting a change, finding that the proposed subsection was not complete. Therefore I have been convinced by the representatives of the people in different provinces of the need to make that subsection even clearer, to include industrial exhibitions together with agricultural, and to make another change which has also been suggested, namely, that the performance shall be deemed to be given without private profit if only individual performers or their agents were paid, provided such fees are not dependent upon the attendance at an exhibition or fair. I shall ask my colleague to move the amendment in order that it may be before the committee. I could say more, but I shall give the right of way to hon. members who desire to present their views, and shall be prepared to give all information required.

speechtext:
termined by Canadian law. But, second, it was clear that the countries which had adhered to the Rome convention had the right with respect to their own nationals to enact so-called domestic legislation, and in the fourth article of the Rome convention it was provided that:
Consequently, apart from the express stipulations of the present convention, the extent of protection, as well as the means of redress secured to the author to safeguard his rights, shall be governed exclusively by the laws of the country where protection is claimed.
That section gave a wide liberty to the parliament of Canada and provided that, except as rights had been stipulated in express terms by the Rome convention, foreign nationals would be subject to the domestic legislation of this country. Furthermore, it was ascertained before the commission, and by evidence given, that no Canadian author was affected because at that date no Canadian author had been admitted as a member of the performing right society of Canada. It was also common ground that copyright in the vast body of these musical works was no longer vested in the original author but had been assigned to the publishers of music at the time or about the time of the first publication of these works; and it appeared that, to a very considerable extent, the whole matter of forming such a combination in Canada rather partook of the nature of a racket in which the publishers of music were to obtain a super-monopoly and control of musical performances in Canada.
But a very considerable part of the complaints against the operations of the Canadian company was due to complaints made by those who broadcast music and by those who receive music by means of broadcast through the receivers for which they obtain dominion licences; and I think one of the main controversies which were from time to time reported to the office of the Secretary of State was with regard to excessive charges made or demanded by the Canadian Performing Right Society from the broadcasting companies as well as those who receive music through the ordinary receiving apparatus. But the Rome convention provided in 11 bis:
(1)	Authors of literary and artistic works shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the communication of their works to the public by radiocommunication.
(2)	The national legislations of the countries of the union may regulate the conditions under which the right mentioned in the preceding paragraph shall be exercised, but the effect of those conditions will be strictly limited to the countries which have put them in force. Such conditions shall not in any
fMr. Caban.]
case prejudice the moral right (droit moral) of the author, nor the right which belongs to the author to obtain an equitable remuneration which shall be fixed, failing agreement, by the competent authority.
The moral right is provided for in article 6 bis of the convention, which is the right of the author to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of the said work which would be prejudicial to his honour or reputation, so that reservation of the moral right of the author does not now concern us, except this, that article 11 bis does provide that by domestic legislation a competent authority may be appointed which shall see that an equitable remuneration may be fixed. Therefore the controversy which arose with respect to the Canadian Performing Right Society has simmered down, in so far as this bill before the committee is concerned, to some way of fixing an equitable remuneration for performing rights such as those which are dealt with by the Canadian company. Under the bill of 1931 it was provided, on the recommendation of the committee of that day, that if complaints were made to the governor in council, then, the governor in council having proceeded by the appointment of a commissioner, and the commissioner having heard the evidence and reported, it would be competent for the governor in council by order of the governor in council to fix the rates of remuneration which were equitable in the case. Complaints came to the notice of the department, and, pursuant to an order numbered 169 dated January 28, 1932, Mr. Justice Ewing was appointed a commissioner to make an inquiry and report, on the petition of six broadcasting stations in the province of Alberta: Edmonton Journal Limited, CJCA; Calgary Herald Limited, CFAC; the Alberta Pacific Grain Company Limited, CKLC; the Albertan Publishing Company Limited, CJCJ; the Voice of the Prairies Limited, CFCN; Lethbridge Broadcasting Limited, CJOC. Evidence was taken by Mr. Justice Ewing, who made a report dated June 29, 1932. Mr. Justice Ewing found that the company, instead of filing a list of the specific musical productions over which it claimed to have copyright, had filed with the Department of Secretary of State catalogues of publishing companies, aild he found that those catalogues included many works in which copyright no longer existed. He says:
A casual examination of the catalogue showed that it contained numerous works of the old masters such as Mendelssohn, Chopin, Beethoven. Mozart. Schubert, Handel. Haydn and Verdi, all of whose works are in the public domain.

Copyright Amendment Act
That is, copyright no longer existed in those works. He continues:
As these catalogues have been sent from England, the representatives of the society at the hearing were unable to offer any explanation. A request for information was cabled to England and a reply was received to the effect that these works had been "rearranged" and that these rearrangements had been copyrighted.
The judge proceeds:
This may or may not be entirely correct, but in any case these catalogues contain musical works which are not in the society's repertoire. For instance, the list contains operettas or operas as a whole whereas the society can only license instrumental excerpts for these operas. The society claims that as a matter of technical compliance with the act it may file lists of works in respect of which it claims this authority to license, and the fact that these lists contain other works over which the society has no control would not affect the filing.
Then in regard to the list of fees filed the judge reports:
In my opinion the intention of the act is- not, as is suggested-that the society shall be permitted to file a list of fees perhaps extravagantly high but at any rate bearing no relationship to the actual fees which the society intends to collect and then to proceed to collect any fee it chooses provided only that such fee is not more than is prescribed in the statement filed.
The judge proceeds to quote the schedule of fees, and he finds that the fees are based upon the power output of the broadcasting station. Then he adds:
The result is that the society has filed a statement of fees for broadcasting stations but it is clear that these are not the fees which it proposes to collect and to that extent it has not complied with clause "B" of section 10 of the act.
The judge then proceeds:
While several matters entered into the fixing of a proper fee to be paid by a broadcasting station for broadcasting copyright music, it was generally admitted that the basic determining factor is the number of people reached by the station in question, that is to say, the "audience."
He proceeds to show that the western companies were being charged approximately the same as the broadcasting companies in the larger centres of Toronto and of Montreal; and he adds:
In fixing the fees the society has left out of consideration the population within the service range of the station. When the facts as to service range, coverage and relative populations were brought out in evidence, the representative of the society very properly admitted that the statement filed was made up without appreciating some of the factors above mentioned as affecting western Canada and this
situation ought to be remedied. Without taking advantage of an admission so made, it must be said that the society has proposed to collect excessive fees from the petitioners.
Then he gives what the society thinks would be a fair price to be charged to certain of these complainants, and he says:
I think it would not be unfair to divide this sum-
That is, the sum claimed:
-by five instead of ten in order to correct the results of inequalities of population.
After receiving this report of Mr. Justice Ewing I was sent by the government as a delegate to Geneva. While there Mr. A. Boosey, who stated to me that he was the executive director of the British company, visited me and discussed the terms of this report. He stated that if the government would refrain from taking action by order in council to fix the limit of the general charges, he would undertake to communicate with his officials in charge of the Canadian company, and see to it that reductions were made in the fees and an amicable adjustment reached on an equitable basis. On his assurance I made no report to council asking for an appropriate order in council to be passed dealing with the Ewing report. But instead of complying with the assurance then given, Which I repeated to the president of the Canadian society in an interview with him after my return, the Canadian Performing Right Society apparently assumed that it could go on making these charges and increasing them at will without making any reasonable effort to come to an amicable understanding with the other interested parties.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO FEES, CHARGES AND ROYALTIES, AND TO CONSTITUTE A COPYRIGHT APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
After the legislation of 1931 was passed the Canadian Performing Right Society filed a tariff of fees, on June 18, 1931. It then filed a supplemental tariff on September 2, 1931; then it changed again by with-
Copyright Amendment Act

drawing the supplemental tariff on the 6th October, 1932. Then, after I had received the assurance of the executive director of the British company which controlled half the shares of the Canadian company, that Mr. Justice Ewing's report would be considered and adjustments would be made in compliance therewith, a further tariff was filed on the 5th January, 1934, dealing only with broadcasting. Then another complete tariff, the third tariff, was filed on the 29th January, 1934, and on March 10, 1934, another amending tariff was filed. On July 11, 1934, another tariff was filed which was limited in its application to public parks, and again on the 12th July, 1934, another tariff was filed with regard to performance of new works.
The general tendency of all these changes was not in compliance with the report of Mr. Justice Ewing but to insist upon a further increase in charges and fees to the broadcasting stations. In the early autumn of 1934 those who were interested in the use of music, broadcasting companies, hotels and other organizations, protested so vigorously that I asked the president of the Canadian Performing Right Society to meet representatives of the broadcasting companies at my office, and they met on October 26, 1934, in Ottawa. I went into the whole matter with the president of the Canadian Performing Right Society in the presence of ten or twelve persons representing these various broadcasting companies and other interested parties. I then agreed, in order that the Canadian Performing Right Society might have a further opportunity to come to an amicable agreement with the broadcasting interests, that I would not ask for an inquiry for a period of three months, in which time I was assured by the president of the Canadian company that efforts would be made to reach an amicable settlement of the difficulties.
This three month period expired on the 26th January, 1935, and I was informed that no agreement had been reached. Yet in the face of the facts as they then existed, and despite the consideration that had been shown from year to year and time to time by the Department of the Secretary of State to the Canadian society, that Canadian society formally filed on the 30th January, 1935, a new tariff, still further increasing the rate and, incidentally, suggesting that they were not going to comply with the request and the suggestion I had made in regard to an amicable settlement. Therefore on the 22nd March, 1935, the governor in council appointed His Honour Judge Parker a commissioner under the Inquiries Act and under the provisions (Of the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931, to

make a further inquiry into the facts and to report. Matters had then reached such a stage that no minister in charge of a department, who had any self-respect at all, could further delay taking action in this matter.
Judge Parker made his report on October 29, 1935, and hon. members will at once perceive that the former Secretary of State had then no official authority in the matter. But I do commend my successor in office that in a matter of great public interest such as this, in respect of which neither of us had any personal interest whatsoever, and in respect of which each of us was merely anxious to preserve and protect the public interest, be proceeded upon receipt of this report to consider ways and means by which the report might be carried into effect. It is not for me to suggest that I might have found other ways and means. But I do personally commend the policy pursued by my successor in this respect, because he has proceeded by this bill to provide for the constitution of an independent tribunal to review complaints. If I had received that report I think, from my knowledge of the facts, that I might have proceeded directly by an order in council fixing the fees. My successor has adopted a rather more conservative course. By this bill he has provided for the appointment of an independent commission to which applications may be made in case excessive and inequitable charges are made by the Canadian Performing Right Society.
Judge Parker reported certain facts. Dealing with the increased rates filed in 1935, he says, on page 34:
A comparison with the fee charged for a one hundred watt station under the 1931 tariff shows a great increase, and the stations required to pay the increased fee naturally objeoted and complained that the new tariff charged was excessive and unreasonable.
That is, the new tariff filed after the previous complaint had been brought to the attention of the Canadian Performing Right Society and after Mr. Justice Ewing's investigation and report. Then a comparison is made between the charges in England and the charges made in Canada, and Judge Parker finds that in view of the scattered population, particularly in the west, it is unfair to charge the same amount per receiving set as is paid in a country so closely settled as Great Britain. He finds that the charge made in Canada should in his opinion be reduced to a rate of 7\ cents per receiving set, which is not very much below the prevalent charge in Great Britain at the time.
Then, again, with regard to the use of these musical compositions in theatres and

Copyright Amendment Act
public buildings of that kind, the Canadian Performing Right Society does- not charge a fixed fee for the performing rights in individual musical compositions, but it charges a rate based upon the entire seating capacity of the theatre or public place in which the performance takes place. And Judge Parker finds in that connection that in the rural districts, the country towns, especially in the country towns of the west, public buildings have been erected and theatres provided for large audiences, exceptional accommodation for exceptional occasions, and because a musical performance may be given to a small audience in one of these larger theatres he finds that it is unfair to charge, not according to the numbers of the audience, not in accordance with the tickets paid for, but upon each seat of the large seating capacity of these buildings whether occupied or not.
Then, with regard to the society's increase of charges, raising a certain minimum fee for matinees and other theatrical performances from S10 to S30, Judge Parker finds that the evidence makes it clear that the raising of the minimum fee was done under pressure of Mr. Mills of the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers. It was not looked upon with favour by the directors of the Performing Right Society of London, England. The raising of the minimum fee in the United States by Mr. Mills was reluctantly followed by the Canadian Performing Right Society. Mr. Jamieson, the president of the Canadian society, however, said in justification, in his evidence, that he regarded the theatre tariff as inadequate and that he only waited to raise the rates in Canada until the rates had been raised in the United States. Then Judge Parker finds that his comparison of the two tariffs shows that in some cases the fees of the Canadian Performing Right Society are higher than those of the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, and in no case are the fees in the 1935 tariff of the Canadian society less than the fees in the 1934 tariff of the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers.
Bearing these facts in mind, and having regard to the fact that ten cents per seat in the past has been acceptable to the Canadian Performing Right Society and was not strenuously objected to by the larger theatres in Canada, he finds that it seems a fair conclusion that the rate of 1931 should not be changed and that the 1935 tariff is unjust and unfair.
Then near the close of his report he says:
... it seems only fair and reasonable that the Canadian Performing Right Society, Limited, should extend that concession-
A certain concession made:
*-to all theatres, and especially to those in the west where they are suffering from drought, and to other places in the east where the towns were dependent upon one industry, and that industry is not now in operation. The theatres were built some time ago and a seating capacity provided when conditions were more prosperous. You have in the maritime provinces, for instance, districts dependent solely upon coal mining and districts dependent solely upon lumbering. Both of these industries, according to the evidence, are at a standstill, and in some localities the percentage of people on relief is very considerable.
I do not think I need proceed further, but I wish to state that when the committee of this house, of which I was chairman, considered the copyright amendment bill of 1931, Mr. H. T. Jamieson, President of the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited, gave his final evidence just before the committee brought its proceedings to a close. Mr. Jamieson stated that certain organizations including the Canadian National Railways and the Toronto Daily Star refused to make contracts with his company until it was placed under government regulations. As chairman of that committee I proceeded to inquire as follows:
Q. Quite so. Do they not attach to their refusal to pay a demand for regulation, that is, as I understand their position, they think that, in case a difference arises with you as to what is a proper compensation, there should be an independent tribunal, by agreement or arbitration or otherwise, to which an appeal could be made to determine whether yqpr demands are reasonable?
A. Well, Mr. Atkinson admitted to me that our tariffs-not demands, our tariffs-were reasonable, and he said it was simply a matter of principle with him, that he would not negotiate with us until we were under government regulation. I said, pay those reasonable tariffs meantime and let us settle the other question later, but they refused.
Q. Just one moment. Is it not a fact-I do not wish to submit the whole record-but is it not a fact that in the evidence before the committee in the British house of Commons it was shown that your British Performing Right Society had entered into contracts for short terms, and at the expiration of those contracts higher rates W'ere demanded, which, in many eases, were regarded by at least the users as exorbitant.
A. Well, sir, there were some increases asked for by the British society, but those increases were asked for only after there had been very considerable accession to the membership for one thing, and only after there had been accessions of many other affiliated European societies.
Q. That, to my mind, represents a valid consideration in support of increasing your royalties and charges, but it is not conclusive as to whether the increases which you demanded under those circumstances, you holding a monopoly, should not be submitted, in case of dispute, to some independent tribunal or to arbitration.
Copyright Amendment Act

A. As Mr. Hawkes could show you in detail, he having knowledge of the operation of the British society, those so-called demands were merely the ideas of the British society as to the increased value of their repertoire.
Q. Why do you refuse really to submit your prices to arbitration, or to the determination of an independent tribunal? I am not here to say that a single charge you ever levied is excessive. But you have a monopoly of 90 per cent of modern music, and, in case of dispute, your views not being accepted by the music user, why should there not be some independent tribunal to which you, as a monopolist with 90 per cent of all modern works in your control, should submit your charges.
The final answer of the witness was:
A. Because we do not know that these rates to be fixed would be fair and reasonable.
The conclusion of the committee was that this being a super-monopoly, combining what had originally been a great number of private monopolies now vested in the Canadian corporation, its charges should be subject to an independent tribunal. That independent tribunal is provided for in the terms of the bill now before the committee.
As the hour is advancing I shall postpone ;o another session a discussion of other matters to which I had intended to refer. At the same time may I commend the principle and policy of the bill-and I speak only for myself and from my own official experience- which the present Secretary of State has introduced for the purpose of creating an independent tribunal to whom those who have grounds for complaint may make such complaints, receive a decision and obtain an equitable adjustment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO FEES, CHARGES AND ROYALTIES, AND TO CONSTITUTE A COPYRIGHT APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, from my
knowledge of the activities and demands of the performing right society I think it might well be compared with a cross-word puzzle. In the first place I doubt very much whether the officials of that society know exactly what they want, and I am quite sure that the public from which it tries to derive its income does not know what it is all about. I question, further, whether hon. members Know the meaning of it.
If the government is desirous of relieving tne public from a great and unnecessary nuisance, it should enact such legislation as would curtail or better regulate the aetivities nl this organization. Since the opening of the session hon. members have been circularized from time to time with literature pertaining to the passage of this bill, -much of which literature has been misleading and incorrect. Certain statements made therein require answering. It was stated that the hotel proprietors had admitted the principle that radio loud speakers in private rooms

should be included in the performing right society licence. The hotel proprietors through their association claim they never made any such admission; yet we know that hon. members have been circularized to the effect that the proprietors had agreed. As they have recorded at their association meetings, the hotel proprietors state that the tariffs filed by the performing right society in 1934 and 1935 are too complicated, and the prices fixed too onerous. Mr. George O'Neil, President of the Ontario Hotel Association, is quoted as saying that the 1934 tariff was satisfactory. Mr. O'Neil's own statement is that he never made any such admission. Mr. O'Neil does not admit that the tariff of 1934 was or is reasonable. Still hon. members have been advised through circulars sent to their office from time to time that Mr. O'Neil and the association had agreed to this kind of thing. That is -the sort of unfair work which has been going on in an effort to put this thing through. The performing right society now admit that the minimum fee of $30 is too high. They are willing to accept $10 when it is paid voluntarily.
His Honour Judge Parker was appointed a commissioner in March, 1935, to conduct an inquiry into this matter. Considerable evidence was taken in various parts of Canada, and in October, 1935, Judge Parker submitted his report. In that Teport he classified the performing right society as a monopoly. In passing, I should like to refer to a statement made by the former Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan). He said that the fee of ten cents per seat was acceptable to the theatre owners. I know for a fact that such is not the case. The theatre owners have protested vigorously against this fee of ten cents per seat. In fact,, they protest against paying anything to this society because they feel that its whole activities are piratical; that it has no licence or right to collect any fee from them. Judge Parker classified this society as a monopoly, and it certainly is a monopoly in every sense of the word, and then some.
I should like to cite one case which came to my personal attention. A certain business man had occasion to employ an orchestra in connection with his restaurant. He was approached by a representative of this performing right Society and told that his fee for the year would be $72. Just how the society arrived at that fee of $72 the restaurant man did not know, and the representative of this society could not tell him. The proprietor of the restaurant said he would not pay it; that he would go to court first, and after considerable dickering the representative of

Copyright Amendment Act
the society took S12 and gave a receipt in full.
I mention this case to justify the statement I made at the outset of my remarks, that the performing right society does not seem to know itself what it is all about or what it wants. It demands $72 of a fee and accepts $12.
As I understand it, the Copyright Act was designed to protect the author and publisher against duplication, publication and distribution. If you purchased a copyrighted book you would not expect to have to pay some society an additional fee because you read it. Country fairs, race tracks and such places are affected by the operations and activities of this organization. The Toronto exhibition bands are concerned, and so on. This society claims the right to step in and collect a fee every time you use a piece of copyright music, which you have already bought and paid for. This is a vicious system of abstracting money from the public.
The tabulated list of music is so lengthy that it is understood only by a few. It is hard to understand just what ,the list does contain. I telephoned the copyright branch in Ottawa a few days ago to ask if certain pieces of music were on the list, and I was advised that they could not tell. I am also informed that no Canadian author or publisher receives one penny of the money thus collected. If you engage an orchestra to furnish entertainment, this society steps in and demands the payment of a fee for every piece of music played, although it has been bought and paid for. When an author produces a piece of music and it is published, the author receives his pay from the publisher and through royalties on the sale of copies of the music. The publisher gets his profit from the sale of copies of the music. But if you or I buy a copy of that piece, take it somewhere and play it in public, we have to pay an additional fee. If we play the piece three, four, five or a dozen times in one evening, we must pay the special fee for every time we play the piece.
If the activities of this society continue, it will not be safe for a man to whistle a tune on the street or play a mouth organ; if he happens to play or whistle one of the pieces on this list, this society could rightly collect a fee from him. In the best interests of an already overburdened public this society should not be allowed to operate in Canada.
