speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for permitting me to interrupt.

I shall not take up very much more of the time of the committee. I want to repeat what I just said, that in the best interests of an already overburdened and overtaxed public, this society should not be allowed to operate in Canada. It is a racket; it is unfair; it is unjust, and it should not be tolerated. Assume that I purchased twenty or thirty copies of a musical orchestration; I pay for them at the regular price, out of which the publisher and the retailer receive their profits. The author receives his payment from the royalties paid. Place that music in the hands of an orchestra and have it played behind closed doors privately, and so far as this association is concerned it is O.K.; but admit the public and in steps the performing right society and demands the payment of a special added fee, not once but for each time a piece of music is played. It is almost im-
Copyright Amendment Act

The ground has been so well covered by those who have preceded me that I shall not delay the committee. I congratulate the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) upon having introduced in this bill one of the recommendations of Judge Parker with respect to the copyright appeal board, and I also congratulate the late government, through its Secretary of State, the present member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan), upon having introduced into the copyright amendment act of 1931 two subsections providing for a stay of proceedings, whereby I take it that we are now

allowed to discuss this question. There are no amendments in the bill now submitted, but though I approve the principle of a copyright appeal board I should like to know whether that board will be easy of access to the small performers or licencees, allowing them to make their complaints in such a way as to secure justice. If this appeal board is to be stationed permanently in Ottawa, it stands to reason that people, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, will have to travel at their own expense to submit their complaints to the board. On the other hand, if the board were itinerant it could go from one end of Canada to t'he other and that would involve an extra charge upon the exchequer of the country. These are the alternatives.
The question is this:	Are we going to pay
just for the benefit of other countries? Every member of this house is aware that not one Canadian author, composer, arranger or publisher gets any benefit from the Copyright Act. Though I congratulate the Secretary of State on having introduced one of the recommendations submitted by Judge Parker, I must say that this will not appease the dissatisfaction which exists in Canada to-day, because out of 10,000 shares, if I may use that term, there are 9,998 that do not belong to this country; and our own Canadian authors, whether they be of Anglo-Saxon origin or French-Canadian, have no show and are not entitled to any share in the profits. There may be four or five who at one time were registered in Washington and obtained American citizenship and they will benefit to a certain extent. But as the saying is, where there is smoke there is fire, and if there is dissatisfaction and suspicion from the Atlantic to the Pacific there must be something wrong. I am not casting reflections on anybody nor am I calling anything a racket; I do not say that there is a nigger in the wood pile. I say, however, that there are thousands of small operators, hotelkeepers, theatre owners, owners of dance halls, and men of initiative who engage orchestras and bands, who are getting no consideration at all. We cannot afford to have unrest in this country at the present time. If even a small proportion of the small operators, the users, the licencees, as the Canadian Performing Right Society wish to term them, express dissatisfaction, it is not for the good of the country that their protests should be disregarded. I say that with a full recognition of the eloquent speeches which have been delivered in this house on behalf of the authors, and I am glad to see that the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Chevrier) is now in his seat. When

Copyright Amendment Act
the hon. member made his plea last February on behalf of the authors, I admit that I fell for it. But are the authors getting the money that they should get? I ask: Are they?
Yes.

Well, let me tell the hon. member that I have before me correspondence which challenges that assertion. How can they get their money? The law requires and each week the Canadian Performing Right Society imposes upon the users the task of making a report of the titles and of the names of the authors, but in this correspondence I have received the writers state that they have made no reports of either titles or authors' names. Under those circumstances how can a proper distribution be made of the moneys collected for the authors? I could refer to some of these letters, but this afternoon it was mentioned that we should not quote newspapers or letters, and I shall abide by the rule even before it is enforced. But the point is: How can the authors, the composers, the arrangers, the publishers, get the amount that they should receive if no report is made of whose music was used? I thought there would be an amendment of this bill this afternoon. Unfortunately there is none. I would have suggested that a committee of this house should have studied the whole problem from A to Z, because there is dissatisfaction, and where there is dissatisfaction there is unrest.
We cannot afford at this time to have our money go without just cause to foreign countries. An analysis made in 1934 of music broadcasted or performed showed that eighty per cent of the fees in respect of our copyrighted music went to the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, which has fifty percent of the shares of the Canadian Performing Right Society. The other part ol the fees being paid to the London Performing Right Society. Now, if eighty per cent goes to the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers and twenty per cent goes to the London Performing Right Society, which includes eighteen affiliated societies, and is where our educational music and training in music comes from, I am unwilling to believe that our money is well spent. I admit, with regard to the creation of the appellate tribunal, that it is an improvement on what the 1931 copyright amendments gave us, but it seems to me that we in Canada are giving money to somebody to take our money away. I ask hon. members to think about this matter to-morrow morning, and decide if I am wrong, because not one composer, not one author in Canada is receiving any benefit.
Our composers, our authors, our arrangers, who give us some nice programs on the radio and in dance halls, concert halls, recreation halls and community halls, do not receive anything. Yet we have to pay just the same to the Canadian Performing Right Society, which is composed fifty-fifty of American authors, composers and publishers, who, by the way, were not parties to the Berne convention and were not even parties to the Rome convention. The Berne convention in 1886 had to do, I believe, with copyright. As far as I understand, the definition of copyright is this: It means the exclusive right of multiplying copies of an original composition. Try to find something else in either the Encyclopaedia Britannica or Larousse; you cannot.
Why does my hon. friend not look into the law? That is the place to find it, not in the dictionary.

But in 1928, let me inform the hon. member, there was a convention in Rome, because the progress of mechanical and electrical instruments had come to the fore. Those who were organized thought they could reap more profit by taking the benefit of anything that was reproduced either mechanically or electrically. But if inventions continue to multiply as they are doing at present, the author of The Peanut Vendor and the author of Yes, We Have No Bananas will be reaping a benefit which no one in this house, no matter how hard he tries to work, can hope to equal. My point is, I think clear. I listened to the speech delivered by the original promoter of the bill, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling), and the speech in rebuttal by the hon. member for Ottawa East, and I was greatly impressed. But I say that the hon. member for Ottawa East has laid too much stress on the Berne convention, the Rome convention, and on what should belong to authors for the product of their genius. If eighty per cent of our money collected under copyright goes to the United States and twenty per cent goes to the London Performing Right Society with the eighteen affiliated societies, the comparison is clear and the conclusion is plain. Where does the educational music come from if not from the old country? The author of Yes, We Have No Bananas is not deserving of so much as the author of In a Monastery Garden, by Ketelby, or the waltzes of Strauss. The small broadcasters, the small performers, the small theatre owners have no option in the choice of their music. Whether they just use music written by Jean-Baptiste Lalonde or Jean-Baptiste Le-
Copyright Amendment Act

francois, jigs and reels, they have to pay the author of The Peanut Vendor, and the authors of the jigs and reels get no reward, as the hon. member for Ottawa East says, for the products of their genius.
I wish to be fair, sir. I have no prejudice. I have heard all the arguments for and against. I have read all the newspapers, and I shall not quote one of them. I have been in that game for the last thirty years as an orchestra leader, a bandmaster and a lealer in reproduction instruments, and I know the game. But I wish to inform the hon. member for Ottawa East, who so ably and so eloquently, on January 19, presented the case for the authors, that although I believe him to be sincere and honest I cannot agree with his arguments, for this reason. Ninety per cent of the time, when an author composes one of these love ballads, he goes to work and sells outright his rights, privileges and everything. Therefore he gets no money afterwards; it goes to those who have organized so as to take these assignments.
Let me conclude my remarks, Mr. Chairman, by saying that I want justice for the publishers and justice for the men who, in a shrewd and businesslike way, have formed this lovely little bit of machinery called the Canadian Performing Right Society. If their cause is just they have my support one hundred per cent, and on the other hand I want justice for the authors, so ably represented by the hon. member for Ottawa East, so long as those authors have the courage to attend an inquiry such as that conducted by Judge Parker and make out their claims. If they do not appear at such an inquiry it must be because they are not interested, and if they are not interested it is because they have assigned their rights, boots, hats, shirts and coats. I wish to be just. Look at all the correspondence I have had in connection with this Canadian Performing Right Society. I shall not quote it, but I shall say this: If you wish peace in this country do not forget the man operating a small theatre, or the man conducting a small dance hall and employing extra help. Do not forget the man who has an orchestra. If he is threatened with a lawsuit and out of that orchestra of six or seven pieces he has to drop one man, you are putting one man out of work. I know it is too late to propose any amendment, but we should have this problem studied by a committee where we could go over the whole matter thoroughly. I should like to do that, because it is my line. We could give justice to everyone; there would be no protests and

no recriminations. If any part of our population figures that it is being discriminated against we are not working for the peace and comfort that we should have in Canada. I should like to talk all night, Mr. Chairman, but I shall not do so.

I had intended originally, Mr. Chairman, to make my remarks on a subject such as that now before the committee somewhat extended, but in view of the fact that at this stage of the session it seems unpopular to make a long speech-I am not so sure that it should not be unpopular at any time during the session-I shall be very brief indeed and simply bring to the attention of the minister and the committee the situation as we find it in the banner county of the Dominion of Canada, the county of Peel.
I should like to preface my remarks by saying that as far as music is concerned we in that county are vitally interested, because there we have annually the largest amateur musical festival put on in any county of its size in the Dominion of Canada. Contributions come from various sources to enable that to be done, and for that reason perhaps I may be excused for telling the committee that the people of my riding are intensely interested in the fact that at various times they have had to pay money to an organization such as the performing right society.
Without going into the legal or constitutional aspect of this matter in any way may I just point out that one of the real difficulties with which the people are faced in connection with these charges is, I believe, the fact that no one seems to know what the charges mean and where the money is going. Perhaps that might appear to be an unfair statement as far as the society is concerned. I have no desire to say anything unfair, but I have in mind particularly four halls in the county of Peel, one in Streetsville, two in Brampton and one in the village of Bolton. The organizations controlling these halls are finding it difficult to make ends meet, as most people who come from rural ridings will understand, and when the performing right society comes to the owners or managers of these halls this is what happens: In the first instance they ask for $30 from these people and finally, in connection with the Orange hall in Brampton, accept an adjustment of something like $25. Then they go to the Odd Fellows' hall in the same town and agree to an adjustment of $14.88. Then they come to the Odd Fellows' hall in Streetsville, in the middle of a dance, and suggest that $2 should be paid and finally

agree to take S10 for the year. In these circumstances perhaps I may be pardoned for suggesting that such practices are scarcely fair to the owners of the halls.
I should like to make a suggestion to the minister. I do not wish to interfere with any legal rights which may belong to the society, but after all I think, if there have to be such charges, there should be some standardized scale of fees. The average person in the country believes that if the society asks for $30 and accepts $14.88, there must be, as my good friend from Verdun (Mr. Wermen-linger) suggests, a nigger in the woodpile somewhere. It is not fair to the performing right society to have that impression abroad. That is something which should be corrected. In addition we have six of the best rural agricultural fairs in the riding. I think, so far as they are concerned, being supported largely by the people of the rural sections, and the halls being kept up by people who have great difficulty in making ends meet, it would be in the interest of all concerned if no fees of any kind were charged to either halls in rural sections or to rural fairs. I make that suggestion without going into any extensive argument, but it is something which should be given consideration. I suggest to the minister that he should make that change so that the people of the rural parts of the dominion will not suffer by virtue of the operations of the performing right society. I have no desire, nor have the people of my county, to avoid paying for something for which we should justly pay, but in the present position they feel that an injustice is being done, and therefore I bring this question to the attention of the minister.
Can the minister inform the committee how much a year the Canadian Performing Right Society is getting out of the country?
I shall note that question. I understand that hon. gentlemen want to speak on the question generally, so perhaps it might be better to finish that part first.

I was going to speak on this subject, but I feel that it is not the time now to go into it. This is too serious a matter to be rushed through in the last moments of the session. But I urge on the minister that this is a very serious matter and we should have a committee to deal with it in the course of the next session if at all possible.

The remarks of my colleague from Peel (Mr. Graydon) lead me to say a few words about the amendment proposed by the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott), with the idea of relieving fairs and exhibitions from the necessity of paying a licence fee. I am entirely in accord with the principle of that amendment, 'but I am not at all sure that the amendment will serve the purpose intended. As hon. members know, these fairs, great and small, from the Toronto exhibition down to the smallest county fair, serve a most excellent object. They are set up for the purpose of encouraging an interest in agriculture, of improving agricultural methods and products, and also of giving a certain amount of diversion and entertainment to a class which gets very little, that is the farmer. The Parker report made it abundantly clear that the feeling of the commissioner was that these fairs, great and small, should not pay a licence fee to the performing right society. That feeling has been expressed in other forms. For instance in Ontario the legislature has relieved all fairs and exhibitions which are conducted by societies set up under the Agricultural Societies Aot, which .includes every fair in Ontario-and it will be found that in other parts of the dominion fairs are set up under similar legislation1-from paying any amusement tax. That provision is found in the Amusements Tax Act of Ontario, R.S.O. 1927, chapter 32, under the regulations which are part of the act, which provides that the following fairs and exhibitions are relieved from paying any tax: Canadian National exhibition, Central Canada exhibition, Western Fair Association, Royal Winter Fair, Ontario Provincial Winter fair, Ottawa Winter fair, and two annual fairs held by any society organized under the Agricultural Societies Act.
Now the objects of the various societies so organized are set out in chapter 71. I shall not read them, because time is passing and we want to get through. But I think I need not stress the fact that these fairs serve a most excellent purpose, and surely these people should be relieved from this tax.
Copyright Amendment Act

The amendment moved by the Postmaster General is, I know, directed towards exempting these fairs and exhibitions from the payment of fees. It does that defining the term "private profit" used in the act. The amendment, if I took it down correctly, reads:
Provided that such performance shall be deemed to be given without private profit if the only fees which are paid are paid to individual performers or their agents.
I urge with all the emphasis I can that that will not have the effect of relieving most of these fairs and exhibitions from payment of a licence fee, for this reason: Most of those fairs and exhibitions, eertainly the larger ones, allow concessions on their grounds, perhaps a small company conducting a sidte show, and the concessionaire will receive profit, which under the amendment I take it would be a fee. In other words, there will be very few fairs in which the only fees paid are paid to individual performers or their agents. If the only fairs and exhibitions which are to be exempt are those which qualify under that amendment I say that these various entertainments will be in just as bad a position as they are in now
It is not as if the performing right society were loath to assert its rights in the courts, because it will be remembered that in 1931 this house made an attempt to do just what we are trying to do now, that is relieve the fairs and exhibitions from the necessity of paying a licence fee, and the ink was hardly dry on the amendment before the society sued the Toronto exhibition. I shall not go into the case, but those interested may find it in 70 Ontario Reports, 34. The result was that the performing right society shot a large hole through the amendment of that date. My submission is that they will be just as zealous in attacking the present amendment. I think we require something better than that. I venture to suggest to the minister that perhaps we have been adopting the wrong touchstone or wrong criterion in determining what is private profit. The point is that all these exhibitions are organized for the purpose of stimulating interest in agriculture and improving agricultural conditions in the districts in which they operate. They are not designed for the purpose of making private profit for anybody. The acts under which they are set up, the Agricultural Societies Act of Ontario, and similar acts in other provinces, provide that if there is any profit resulting from the fair or exhibition such profit shall be devoted to the purposes of the society. That is to say, the profit shall be held from one year and used the next year. But it is not private profit for any person. It may be returned to the authority, whether

dominion, provincial or municipal, which makes a grant in aid. Practically all these exhibitions receive help from one governmental source or another. I submit it is not a matter of importance that some minor concessionaire on the grounds makes a small profit or that he does not, and it certainly is very undesirable that the fact that some such small operator does make a profit should render the exhibition or fair subject to licence. That is good. I move:
That section 1 of Bill 55, an act to amend the Copyright Amendment Act 1931, be amended by substituting for subsection (viii) the following subsection, namely:
(viii) The performance without private profit of any musical work at any agricultural, or agricultural and industrial exhibition or fair which is held under or receives a grant from or is promoted by dominon, provincial or municipal authority, provided that such performance shall be deemed to be given without private profit, if the only profit accruing to the society, board, or corporation or other authority holding the exhibition or fair is applied in the furtherance of the general purposes for which such society, board, corporation or other authority is constituted, or has returned to any dominion, provincial or municipal body such grant of money in aid of the said exhibition or fair.
The amendment will protect these fairs, great and small, and I submit they have a right to protection. The hour is late, and I shall not enlarge upon my observations.

It is regrettable that we
should be kept here at this late hour. The bill went to the committee two months ago, and as we have not been swamped with legislation I think it might have been considered earlier. Notwithstanding some observations made to-night I should like to share the views of some hon. members that the work and genius of a composer are his personal property to dispose of as he pleases. It is unfortunate that Canadian authors and composers have been forced out of the picture. The only way in which they could possibly get into the picture would be through the operation of the Canadian Performing Right Society, which is not a very happy avenue of recovery. This would more properly be entitled a bill to control the operations of the Canadian Performing Right Society than an amendment to the Copyright Act.
Probably there is not a member in the house who has not received some sort of protest from some portion of the dominion against the arbitrary activities of the Canadian Performing Right Society. We may admit that such a society is necessary. There are performing right societies in England and in other European countries. Then there was the Havana convention which takes in the South American countries.
The operations of the Canadian Performing Right Society have prompted a great deal of antagonism and, as I have said, there have been protests from practically every portion of the dominion. If those complaints are justified they exist simply by reason of .the fact that this parliament has made them possible because of the statute. By the same token parliament can remove the difficulties; it can remove any cause for complaint against the operation of the Canadian Performing Right Society.
As early as February, I received complaints from my district. We ought to get away from the legal aspect of the question, if we can, and get the views of the man on the street,
the man who does not understand what all this means. Copyright legislation does not appeal to many of us, but this bill is a matter of real interest to every hon. member because it affects every constituency, every municipality large or small, every community in which there is a broadcasting station, a theatre, a hotel, a restaurant, a skating rink, an entertainment hall or any public place in which music is played. The Canadian Performing Right Society is simply a subsidiary of the American Society of Authors, Composers and Publishers, and of the Performing Right Society of England, with the latter of which are affiliated the various societies throughout Europe. Each country gives these societies authority to issue licences and to collect fees for the performance of music. They saw that apparently Canada was a fertile field, and the Canadian Performing Right Society was organized. What were the assets? It was simply an assignment of the alleged control of two million pieces of music. No person knows whether those who assigned them to the Canadian Performing Right Society had any title to them. That society to-day does not know to what music it has title; it could not tell you, under any circumstances. But it is quite willing to assume that everything in the air belongs to it. They continued such arbitrary actions as the issuing of licences and the collection of fees. They fixed a minimum charge of $10 per annum. They virtually said to users of music in Canada: We control from two to three million pieces of music; some time within the twelve months to follow you will use some of those pieces; we shall not be there to check you up, so we are going to charge you a minimum of $10 per annum. There was not much said about this charge. As a matter of fact, the public generally were not cognizant of the operations of the society. But they became cognizant in 1935 when this minimum charge was raised to $30.
Forget about the large restaurant or hotel in the east, but think what this means to the modest restaurant or hotel in the west. A representative of the performing right society walks in and tells the proprietor that he w'ants $10. He shows him a list of the cases they have successfully prosecuted. The restaurant man does not know exactly what he is paying the $10 for, but this collection is always punctuated with a legal threat. The representative comes in again and asks for $30. When he is asked why, he simply says that they have raised the rates. That is all there is to it, and if the man will not pay, they threaten to sue. Such operations do not tend to promote very good feeling. You are
Copyright Amendment Act

required to make an application and attached to the application form or the bill or whatever it is, in many instances, are slips of paper showing the various cases which have been successfully prosecuted. Whenever authors or composers pool their works in such a society, it becomes inevitably a monopoly. This monopoly increased its rates and the result was the appointment of Judge Parker as a royal commissioner to make an investigation. To some extent, this bill is based upon the recommendations of Judge Parker.
This performing right society with its usual arbitrary attitude does not admit the right of this parliament to fix its rates or to interfere in any way with its operations. These operations are being conducted by virtue of the provisions of the Copyright Act, which permits the society to issue licences and to collect fees, and I submit that this parliament, therefore, has authority to remedy the arbitrary tactics of the society. The society takes refuge behind the fact that Canada is a signatory to the Berne convention. That may be so, but there is no obligation in that convention which delegates to this society or any similar society in another country the power to fix or regulate rates. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said, the Berne convention gives the signatories all the rights and privileges of the other countries which are signatories in so far as the copyright laws of those countries govern. In other words, as has been stated before, the recognition of possession, the extension of protection and the means of redress are governed entirely and exclusively by the copyright laws of the country in which such redress is sought.
We come now to England. I must say that the Performing Right Society in England1 did not approve the Canadian Performing Right Society raising its rates, but the American company which practically controls the situation told the Canadian directors to put on more pressure and get more money. So the fees were arbitrarily increased to a minimum of $30. It must be remembered that that is a minimum charge, the fee being raised in accordance with the returns on the various pieces of music which are played. In the old country the rates are arranged to some extent by negotiation or arbitration, but in this country there has been no such thing as negotiation between the Canadian Performing Right Society and users of music. The society simply say: We want so much or we will sue you. Even with the arbitration and negotiation that went on in the old country, there were protests against the fees charged. Only recently the British Board of
[Mr. EslingJ
Trade made a recommendation to His Majesty's government that the British delegates to the forthcoming convention in Brussels should indicate to the convention that where excess charges are made by bodies which control a number of copyrights, legislation be brought down to do away with the copyright monopoly.
While the bill introduced by the minister may appear on its surface to have some merit, I am absolutely opposed to any further expenditure of money from the public treasury for the purpose of facilitating the collection of fees by the Canadian Performing Right Society. That is all it amounts to. This society has been so arbitrary in its actions as to require the expenditure of some $17,000 for the purpose of conducting an inquiry by a royal commissioner, and the appeal board set up by this bill will mean an expenditure of some $30,000 or $40,000 per annum.

Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to correct him? The members of the board will receive no remuneration. I am presenting an estimate of $1,000 to cover expenses for the coming year, which figure is far from the figures mentioned by my hon. friend.

I shall accept the minister's explanation. It may be that the members of this board will receive no remuneration, but they will receive travelling and living expenses. I do not think the minister believes for one moment that all the disputes in connection with hotels, restaurants and broadcasting stations will be settled in Ottawa. That is not the intention of this bill as it provides that the members of the board shall receive travelling and living expenses. To receive those expenses in connection with a federal activity is a pretty good job at any time, even without salary. In addition to the travelling and living allowances to be paid to the members of this board, there will be the fees for the experts who appear before the board. Who will those experts be? They will be the representatives of the Canadian Performing Right Society who will appear before the board to try to prove that their fees are moderate and within reason. They will be paid from the federal exchequer.
Let us look at this matter from another angle. Why should1 the Secretary of State not appoint from his own department someone thoroughly familiar with the act, or why should the Minister of Transport not appoint a member of his department thoroughly familiar with radio and, to be fair, appoint a third member from the Canadian Performing Right Society? In view of the fact that

Copyright Amendment Act
this bill is intended to smooth out the wrinkles I suggest that the performing right society should foot the bil'l. There is no reason why one dollar should come out of the federal treasury in order to carry out the purposes of the act.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St.George has pretty well gone over the question of fees. No one knows anything about fees. The hon. member for Ottawa East will no doubt give us to-morrow a very full refutation of the adverse criticism made to-night, but what do we find in connection with fees? I submit that we are on very good ground when we take Judge Parker's report and any evidence submitted during the course of his investigation, and he shows that the society is collecting on the basis of ten cents for every receiving set in the dominion. If you inquire from the radio department you will find that there are about a million of which they have knowledge and a few hundred thousand more about which they do not know; you may be sure that the performing right society does not overlook any number of receiving sets, and their fees are allocated accordingly. But in the old country, instead of ten cents the fee is only 7| eents. What the man in the restaurant, what the man who runs an hotel or a skating rink says is this: "I have paid for a federal licence for my radio and the broadcasting station pays ten cents for every receiving set in Canada. Of what use' is my radio if I must pay for the music that comes out of it?" The situation is ridiculous. If the broadcasting stations did not pay a blanket rate, the matter would be different. Take skating rinks. They can use only half a dozen records or so. They use gramophone records on which royalty has been paid, and these records are adapted to a certain rhythm for skating. They have loud speakers and they play the music over and over again. Well, they want to know why they should have to pay a minimum fee of $30 a year to the performing right society.
I would not hesitate to accord to that society every consideration in the world if there were Canadian authors or composers participating in the revenues collected by the society. As a matter of fact the society has said: "We are extending an invitation to Canadian authors and composers." Yes, they did, but only since Judge Parker submitted his report, because he said that in 1934 he could not find that one dollar went direct to a Canadian author, composer or publisher. It is true that some of them joined the society in the United States, and I know that to-day some Canadian authors are being invited to join.
I want to say one thing in conclusion. I am going to advocate that when this society goes to any man to collect $30, it should be required to present him with a list of the compositions to which it claims title. It is only since this house met that the amateur dramatic society of Toronto wanted to put on the Pirates of Penzance, and what happened? They wanted to broadcast it for seven minutes and the president of the dramatic society said: "We shall have to go to the performing right society and ascertain .what we have to pay them." Well, they found that the fee was $61 for seven minutes, but the broadcasting station said no, and they put the matter into the hands of a solicitor and discovered that the Pirates of Penzance was in the public domain. The performing right society had no copyright in it. If that is done in one case, is it not reasonable to suppose that the people throughout the dominion have been generally mulcted? Those who come from the prairies know what it means for a man to put his brand on a steer that does not belong to him. There is a distinct place in society for such a man. Is there any difference between putting your brand on a steer that does not belong to you and putting your brand on music that is not your property and attempting to collect a fee for the use of it?
